Iran : Téhéran propose un accord, Trump menace de «faire sauter» le pays
items.description: Entre negociations et menaces, Washington et Teheran continuent de souffler le chaud et le froid. L'Iran a confirme mercredi 30 septembre avoir recu, par l'intermediaire du Qatar, une reponse officielle americaine a sa derniere proposition destinee a mettre fin a sept mois de guerre. Le contenu de cette reponse n'a pas ete rendu public. Le plan iranien prevoit notamment un retour progressif a une circulation normale dans le detroit d'Ormuz, passage strategique pour le commerce mondial des hydrocarbures. En echange, Teheran reclame la levee de sanctions, le deblocage de ses ports et la restitution d'avoirs geles. Washington avait rejete une premiere version de ces conditions, mais les discussions se poursuivent avec la mediation du Qatar et du Pakistan. Trump fait du Trump C'est dans ce contexte que Donald Trump a de nouveau durci le ton. Interroge sur la suite du conflit, le president americain a presente deux issues possibles : « soit nous concluons un accord, soit nous les faisons sauter ». Il a ajoute que la guerre prendrait fin « tres bientot, d'une maniere ou d'une autre », sans preciser quelle option Washington privilegiait. Cette menace survient alors que les etats-Unis accentuent parallelement leur pression economique. Washington a annonce de nouvelles sanctions dans le cadre de l'operation « Economic Outcast », visant les chaînes d'approvisionnement de l'appareil militaire iranien. L'economie iranienne est deja lourdement affectee par le conflit, les sanctions et les restrictions pesant sur ses ports. Malgre cette rhetorique, la voie diplomatique reste ouverte. Teheran affirme avoir transmis de nouvelles propositions, tandis que les mediateurs poursuivent leurs echanges avec les deux camps. Le detroit d'Ormuz demeure au cœur des negociations : sa reouverture complete constitue a la fois un levier pour l'Iran et une priorite pour Washington.

items.title: Utap | Pas de sécurité alimentaire sans préservation des filières agricoles
items.description: L’Union tunisienne de l’agriculture et de la pêche (Utap) a appelé les pouvoirs législatif et exécutif à renforcer le soutien aux agriculteurs et aux marins-pêcheurs, à réunir toutes les conditions d’une meilleure production, et à adopter des mesures et des mécanismes capables de protéger les filières nationales et de renforcer leur résilience. Ces actions visent à contribuer à la souveraineté alimentaire, à soutenir l’économie nationale et à préserver les intérêts des producteurs. Dans un communiqué publié par son bureau exécutif national à l’issue de sa réunion périodique tenue hier, mercredi 30 septembre 2026, à son siège, l’organisation syndicale a souligné la nécessité de conjuguer les efforts de toutes les parties prenantes afin de garantir un démarrage réussi de la campagne céréalière 2026-2027, en assurant, notamment, la disponibilité des intrants agricoles — en particulier les semences et les engrais — ainsi que leur bonne distribution et leur acheminement vers les bénéficiaires dans les délais impartis, limitant ainsi les pratiques de monopole et de spéculation tout en créant les conditions propices à la réussite de la saison. Il a réitéré son appel à annoncer, dès le début de la campagne, une augmentation du prix de référence à la réception des céréales, afin d’offrir aux agriculteurs une visibilité claire, de les inciter à étendre les superficies cultivées et de soutenir la production nationale, renforçant ainsi l’autosuffisance et réduisant le recours aux importations. Concernant la filière des dattes, l’Union a souligné la nécessité d’une coordination précoce entre les différentes parties prenantes et de la mise en œuvre de mesures garantissant les ressources financières indispensables aux opérations de stockage, de commercialisation et d’exportation. Ces actions doivent contribuer à une gestion optimale de la récolte, à l’équilibre entre l’offre et la demande, à la stabilité des prix ainsi qu’à la pérennité de la filière, lui permettant de préserver sa position et de continuer à jouer son rôle dans l’économie nationale. Par ailleurs, l’Utap a exprimé son opposition aux importations inconsidérées de fruits et légumes, en raison des répercussions directes qu’elles pourraient avoir sur les filières de production nationales et les intérêts des producteurs, appelant à revoir la stratégie d’importation afin de répondre aux besoins du marché sans nuire à la production locale, de protéger les agriculteurs contre une concurrence déloyale et de garantir la pérennité de l’activité et de la production. Concernant la filière de l’huile d’olive, l’Union a indiqué qu’elle suivait de près l’évolution du marché mondial en termes de production et de prix. Elle a appelé les producteurs à faire preuve de prudence dans les opérations de récolte et de commercialisation, et à ne pas se laisser entraîner par des rumeurs visant à faire chuter les prix à la production, à influencer le marché et à porter préjudice aux intérêts des producteurs. L’Office de l'huile a également été appelé à assumer son rôle national en suivant l’évolution du marché et en prenant les mesures nécessaires pour contribuer à la stabilité des prix et à la protection des intérêts des producteurs. Concernant le secteur de la pêche, l’Utap a exprimé son indignation face à l’exclusion délibérée, par l’autorité de tutelle, des professionnels du secteur des commissions techniques traitant des questions maritimes, soulignant que la présence des professionnels et de leurs représentants dans les différents processus de concertation et d’élaboration des décisions relatives au secteur est indispensable pour garantir l’efficacité de ces décisions et leur adéquation avec la réalité du métier. Elle a également réaffirmé son refus des décisions unilatérales susceptibles de porter préjudice au service public maritime et aux intérêts des professionnels, tout en réitérant son attachement au dialogue, à la concertation et à l’adoption d’une approche participative pour traiter les dossiers en question. items.title: Malgré les polémiques, Le Pen reste en tête, Philippe progresse, la gauche recule
items.description: Le compte a rebours est lance vers le 18 avril 2027. Creditee de 31 % a 36 % des intentions de vote selon les configurations, Marine Le Pen fait toujours la course en tete. Sa quasi-stabilite (entre -1 et 0 point) impressionne, alors que le terrain n'a expose qu'un tiers des sondes aux revelations de Mediapart sur de vieux ecrits attribues a Jordan Bardella . 📊 La vague 6 du baromètre Ifop- @Fiducial pour @LCI , @Le_Figaro et @SudRadio confirmerait la nette avance de Marine Le Pen. Créditée de 31% à 36% des intentions de vote au 1er tour, elle devancerait systématiquement le candidat arrivé en 2e position de 11 à 19 points. pic.twitter.com/obdr1z2ImL — Ifop Opinion (@IfopOpinion) September 30, 2026 edouard Philippe, donne entre 16 % et 21 %, reprend des couleurs. Chaque fois qu'il est teste, le maire du Havre se qualifie pour le second tour. Face a Gabriel Attal, il fait deux fois mieux (16 % contre 8 %). Frederic Dabi, de l'Ifop, y voit « un debut de decantation dans le bloc central » alors que la tournee des bistrots de Gabriel Attal vire au fiasco . 🔴🍺 INSOLITE | L’opération « 1000 bistrots » de Gabriel Attal ne mobilise visiblement toujours pas les foules, comme ici à Garches. (Député Pierre Cazeneuve) pic.twitter.com/CjfxFE11hP — French Report (@french_report78) September 27, 2026 a gauche, Jean-Luc Melenchon conserve la premiere place du camp progressiste (14 % a 17 %), mais glisse d'un a deux points et ne se qualifie plus pour le second tour dans aucune des dix hypotheses testees… Mais il y a trois jours, une autre etude d'opinion le donnait au second tour dans toutes les configurations, ce qui invite a la prudence. Raphael Glucksmann, estime entre 9 % et 13 %, reste le mieux place des candidats a la primaire sociale-democrate, loin devant Olivier Faure ou Segolene Royal (3 % a 4 %). Bruno Retailleau (LR) oscille entre 5 % et 11 %, tandis qu'eric Zemmour stagne entre 3 % et 4,5 %. Le sondage, realise du 25 au 29 septembre aupres de 1 393 personnes, laisse encore ouvert le match pour la deuxieme place, mais confirme pour l'instant la solidite de Marine Le Pen et la dynamique favorable a edouard Philippe.

items.title: Messi to receive honorary doctorate from Argentine university
items.description: Retiring Argentina captain Lionel Messi is set to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires (UBA) in recognition of his football career and contribution to the country. The university’s Higher Council unanimously approved the conferment of the honorary degree, which is its highest honorary distinction. The award will be presented to Messi on Tuesday, October 6, ahead of Argentina’s farewell match against Benin at the Monumental Stadium. UBA said Messi’s career represented “excellence, perseverance, humility and ethical practice”, while also highlighting his commitment to representing Argentina. The university cited his role in Argentina’s major international triumphs, including the 2021 Copa América, 2022 Finalissima, 2022 FIFA World Cup and 2024 Copa América. It also recognised Argentina’s run to the 2026 World Cup final. UBA Rector Ricardo Gelpi said the institution wanted the recognition to go beyond Messi’s statistics and achievements on the football pitch. “Beyond what all Argentinians know about Messi, regardless of the numbers and statistics that attest to his status as an athlete, we also want to recognise a humble, persevering person, an example and ambassador of our popular culture and national identity,” Gelpi said. He added that the honour was also intended to acknowledge Messi’s broader influence through sport and his representation of Argentina. UBA Vice-Rector Emiliano Yacobitti said the distinction recognised the values Messi had displayed while representing the national team. “Leo Messi knew how to convey the values of the Argentine jersey and represent it with courage and respect, and thus managed to take it to the highest level of world football. “But this Honorary Doctorate is a recognition that transcends his football career. It is a tribute and a thank you that we offer him from the UBA, on behalf of all of Argentine society,” Yacobitti said. The university said honorary doctorates are part of a long-standing tradition among leading institutions of higher education, allowing them to recognise individuals whose achievements and influence extend beyond their professional fields. The honour comes as Messi prepares for his Argentina farewell against Benin on October 6 at the Monumental Stadium. The match is expected to mark his final appearance for the national team. The post Messi to receive honorary doctorate from Argentine university appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Prix des produits: intensification des opérations de contrôle dans le Zondoma
items.description: (Zondoma, le 01 Octobre 2026) Dans le cadre de la lutte contre les pratiques commerciales illicites et de la protection des consommateurs, la Direction régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat du Yaadga (DRICA-YAADGA) a mené, du 26 au 29 septembre 2026, une opération de contrôle économique dans la province du Zondoma. Les équipes sont intervenues notamment à Kera-Douré, Bassi, Saye et Gourcy. Au total, 141 commerçants ont été contrôlés et 19 points de vente scellés. Les opérations ont concerné les produits de grande consommation, les débits de boissons ainsi que les stations-service. Les contrôles ont également permis de saisir des cartouches de cigarettes frauduleuses, 17 fûts de cyanure, des médicaments prohibés, des boissons frelatées et une importante quantité de produits périmés. À travers ces opérations, la DRICA-Yaadga poursuit ses actions de contrôle en vue de faire respecter la réglementation, d’assainir le marché et de protéger les consommateurs. Les contrevenants s’exposent aux sanctions prévues par les textes en vigueur. Pour toute plainte ou dénonciation, les consommateurs peuvent appeler les numéros verts 80 00 11 84 / 80 00 11 85 / 80 00 11 86. DCRP/MICA DRICA/Yaadga L’article Prix des produits: intensification des opérations de contrôle dans le Zondoma est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Ligue pro: Génération Foot, très loin d’être prête
items.description: Reprise tardive et effectif très jeune, sans cesse renouvelé : à quelques jours du début du championnat, l’entraîneur des Grenats de Deni Biram Ndao, Pape Boubacar Gadiaga, estime que son équipe est loin d’être à 100 %. « Nous rencontrons beaucoup de difficultés dans notre jeu, car nos exigences sont élevées: nous devons courir davantage, conserver le ballon, commettre moins de fautes techniques et être moins fatigués que l’adversaire », avait-il réagi après la lourde défaite contre Guédiawaye (0-3) en présaison. Serein, il rappelle que le groupe est en phase d’apprentissage. « Il reste encore du travail à accomplir et des étapes à franchir », reconnaît-il. Il avance deux explications : la reprise tardive des entraînements et le renouvellement constant de l’effectif, avec la montée de pépites en équipe A. Physiquement, seuls quelques joueurs peuvent tenir 80 à 90 minutes à haute intensité. « Nos débuts de saison sont souvent difficiles parce que nous disposons d’un effectif très jeune, constamment renouvelé, et nous n’avons jamais les huit semaines de préparation nécessaires pour être à 80 % du rythme dès le départ », insiste-t-il. Le club ne compte que trois à quatre semaines de travail. Lorsque la préparation déborde sur les premiers matchs officiels, prévient-il, l’équipe perd des points sur des détails et la confiance s’effiloche. Il promet pourtant un groupe meilleur d’ici deux semaines, le temps de corriger les lacunes. Sur le podium puis 4e lors des deux dernières saisons, Génération Foot, qui recevra l’As Pikine en ouverture, ne sera pas en reste dans la course au titre. Mais son entraîneur n’en fait pas une obsession. « Au Sénégal, toutes les équipes pensent au titre, car le championnat manque parfois de logique et le dernier peut battre le premier chez lui avec la manière », constate-t-il. La priorité reste la formation des jeunes et une bonne figuration en coupes nationales, avec l’espoir de voir les jeunes promus prendre leurs responsabilités après le départ de véritables leaders. Par Mohamed DIENE (Correspondant à Rufisque)

items.title: Min Jin Lee’s Underdog Morality
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts If there is a villain in Min Jin Lee’s new novel, American Hagwon , it’s Danbi, a young woman who seduces married men, frames a co-worker for sexual harassment, and embezzles money. But as with Lee’s earlier, breakout epic novel, Pachinko , this one has no real villains. Danbi, like most people in Lee’s novels, is moved by larger forces: a rural childhood, an alcoholic stepfather, and a desperate need to survive in the face of a looming economic crisis. American Hagwon takes place during the Asian financial crisis of 1997 and follows a group of interconnected families moving among South Korea, Australia, and the United States. A hagwon is a private tutoring center and the repository of the Korean families’ anxieties about ensuring future success for their children. Lee’s landscape makes room for Dickensian-style urchins, such as a 9-year-old girl shipped alone to a boarding house in California so she can study hard and get into UC San Francisco, and also humane tutors who make it their mission to more deeply engage their young students and encourage parents to ease off. Lee approaches her characters in the same way as the social realists of the 19th century, such as George Eliot, Charles Dickens, and Leo Tolstoy. She subjects ordinary people to forces that test them—in this case, a Korean system that perceives elite education as almost an amulet against failure, putting tremendous financial and emotional pressure on both children and parents. But that doesn’t make her a relativist. “I’m definitely a moral novelist,” Lee says on Radio Atlantic . “You know why? Because, actually, I think most people are desperate for morality.” In this episode, Lee talks about what led her to write the book, including her own path through the American school system, her mother’s laissez-faire approach to school, and her hundreds of interviews with Korean parents, students, and hagwon teachers. And she reflects on the central theme of all of her novels, which is the displacement of people: “I think diaspora is now the modern person’s permanent condition,” she says in the podcast. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: This September, my youngest child went to college, and the experience for me was very different than when I sent my other two children to college. With them, I didn’t question the decision all that much. They got in somewhere. We celebrated. Off they went. But now it’s 2026, and college is a loaded word—more expensive than ever and its value not as clear. At this moment, no honest parent can easily answer the question: What’s the relationship between a child’s education, and their future success and happiness? [ Music ] I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . The world has waited almost 10 years for a new novel by Min Jin Lee. In 2017, she published the best-selling historical epic Pachinko . It became a National Book Award finalist, it was named one of The New York Times ’ 100 best books of the 21st century, and it was adapted into a series for Apple TV . Her first book since Pachinko is out this week. It’s called American Hagwon , hagwon meaning “private tutoring center” in Korean. Min Jin Lee: Do you want me to tell you how to say hagwon ? Just like Hanna . Rosin: Ho -gwon. Lee: Does that make sense? Rosin: Is it the speed of it? Ha gwon? Lee: No. Like, you know how you can say Ha- nnah or Ho -nna? Rosin: It’s Ho -gwon. Lee: You say Ho -nna. Rosin: Yes. Lee: It’s exactly like that. It’s Ho -gwon. Ho -gwon. Rosin: Yeah, Ho -gwon. Rosin: Lee spent years researching and conducting hundreds of interviews with Korean parents, students, and hagwon teachers. The novel follows a group of interconnected families who move between Korea, Australia, and the U.S. Like Lee’s previous books, Christianity, morality, and immigration are major themes in Hagwon. But its central preoccupation is education: The lengths that Korean parents will go to to get their children into elite schools, their sacrifices—financial and emotional—and how they affect both the parents and the children, all set against the backdrop of the 1997 Asian financial crisis, which adds an edge of desperation to their quest for success. Min Jin Lee joins me today to talk about life in the shadow of school. Rosin: Min, welcome to the show. Lee: Thank you, Hanna. Rosin: So as I was reading about you, I discovered something that made me so happy, which is that you and I have extremely similar immigrant journeys. We are exactly the same age. We came to America at exactly the same time, both moved to Queens, and I went to Stuyvesant and you went to Bronx Science. We missed by a hair being high-school classmates. Lee: And you know, I could have gone to Stuyvesant ’cause I got in, but then my older sister went to Bronx Science, and I was bullied so much as a kid, and she protected me, so people just said, my parents and everybody else agreed, She should go to school with her sister . Rosin: For people who don’t know Stuyvesant and Bronx Science, how should we describe them? They’re like the launchers of immigrants, I feel like. Lee: Yes, if you’re very lucky. Rosin: Yes, if you get in. They’re magnet schools, and if you happen to pass—they are hagwon-like—if you manage to pass the test, the one critical test, you're one lucky immigrant. . But the thing I wanted to talk about was not Stuyvesant but Queens, because I so rarely meet people in my life who grew up in Queens. Lee: Really? Rosin: Yeah. And I go back to Queens a lot. My family still lives there. The overwhelming feeling I have in Queens is that everybody there is displaced and carries the feeling of displacement, even if they move somewhere else or do something else. It’s just, like, an entire borough of people who are in the wrong place. And I just wondered if you shared that as someone who grew up in the same era that I did. Lee: I completely agree. And then also, even if you don’t feel that, everybody you care about is like that. So you can’t help but feel this way. Rosin: Yeah. I mean, I lived in just, like, a mixed immigrant neighborhood. And it sounds like you lived in a—no, you didn’t live in a Korean neighborhood. Lee: There’s so many. Like, I didn’t know white people existed. Rosin: You did not? Lee: No. You know why? Because nobody was white. You were from Pakistan. You were from India. You were from all these different countries, so you always had a country affiliation. So even if you were white you would say, I’m Polish . Rosin: Yeah. Lee: I’m Italian . I’m Irish . Rosin: Yes. Lee: And if you spoke Spanish, whatever country you came from, they’re like, Oh, he’s Spanish, and you’re like—and then you don’t think about the country, you think like, Oh, no, actually he’s from Ecuador . Rosin: Right. Lee: But then if you’re from, let’s say, the Dominican Republic, you’re like, “Oh, no, I am not Puerto Rican.” Rosin: Yes. Yes. That was actually the big battle in my middle school, was between Dominicans and Puerto Ricans. Lee: Yeah, DR, PR. Rosin: And the big thing was lunch. That’s what I remember. Like, it was What language you speak? and What did you bring to school for lunch? That’s where all the divides came in. Anyway, okay, to your novel. I did an informal survey of friends, and I would say less than half of them knew what the word hagwon meant, nor did they understand the whole culture of hagwon and what comes along with that word, so I think we need to start there. What is it? Lee: So a hagwon is a learning center. Anytime you pay somebody to teach you something that’s not in regular school, that’s a hagwon. So in Korea, everybody goes to hagwons. The elderly, the child, the middle-aged person goes to hagwon to learn gourmet cooking, tap dancing, singing. Rosin: But this makes it sound lovely, like a hagwon. Lee: No, it is actually lovely. Because you have the optionality of self-improvement, and that’s very normal. And then you also have hagwons for civil-service exams, as well as when you’re 4 years old, you go to hagwon to learn English. So that’s the hagwon that people are really—I think Americans get really upset about. Rosin: Ah. And I know you did a lot of research into hagwons. Can you just talk about the range? Like, was there a memory as you were looking into hagwons where you thought, Oh, this is very stressful , and other times when you thought, Oh, this is lovely? Lee: Oh. I think before I started the research, I thought it was very stressful because I read all the data, and the data is terrifying. So, like,, 80 percent of Koreans send their 5-year-olds to hagwon. So as a Western person, as an immigrant, as an American, you’re kinda going, “That’s kind of a lot.” Rosin: Yeah. Lee: And also, you learn that the middle income of a Korean person was, let’s say, $35,000, and you’re spending $400 a month to hagwon bills for your 4-year-old, which apparently explains the low birth rate and the low marriage rate of Korea. So I found that really stressful. And then, of course, I go to all the different hagwons, and I don’t feel stressful at all. Rosin: Oh, interesting. Lee: Because they’re so normal. And then even the hagwons in America, I thought they’re actually necessary. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I did a complete 180. Rosin: Really? So you started out with the stereotype of hagwons— Lee: Yes, based on the data. Rosin: —like this is torturing children. They are— Lee: Don’t get a childhood. Rosin: They don’t get a childhood. They’re not able to play. Lee: All of it. Rosin: They’re being crammed with information. And that is not what you came out thinking? Lee: I do not believe that anymore. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I don’t think that they’re lovely, but I see why they’re necessary. Rosin: Even if it means that children. I mean, my stereotype, and I’ve visited Korea, so I know a little bit, is that it’s the number of hours, it’s the quantity of hours you are expected to spend in school. Lee: Yeah. And I think that if you’re a working parent and you have kids, hagwons are a kind of child care. And also, because you can’t help the kids with homework, so then parents will actually outsource this, and it becomes a low-cost way to get tutoring. So if you think about it that way, all of a sudden, every working parent in America is like maybe, Why don’t I do that? Rosin: Yeah. It’s like high-end aftercare. Yeah. It’s— Lee: —all very good. Well, it’s kinda like Kumon. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Kumon is very inexpensive in America. And if your kid does Kumon, then you could be a legal secretary or somebody’s assistant-chief-of-staff kind of person and say, “You know, that’s $400 a month. I make $80,000 a year, and my kid can do these worksheets, get the stickers and the stuffed animals, and the kid will be probably in the top 10 percent of my public school.” Rosin: Okay. So in the novel, there’s a mixed portrait. So for example, there’s a character named Ginny. And she’s almost a Dickensian character. She feels the most Dickensian of your characters. She’s sort of an urchin. You know, she’s sent by her parents at 9 years old to the U.S. Her sole mission is to get into UCSF and go to medical school and be a doctor, but that means she ends up at a boarding house. Where does this child come from, and what does she represent? Lee: They’re all around us, these kids. So sociologists call them “parachute children.” And they usually come from East Asia, and they’re parachuted down to another country, not necessarily always America—’cause America’s actually quite expensive—and the person who takes care of them is called the “homestay person,” the guardian. And you can pay somebody that you know or a family member, and you pay room and board. However, if you don’t have the money to pay, where does this child go? Rosin: So you just said that to me pretty neutrally, as if there’s no heartbreak involved in the story of Ginny. Is that actually how you feel or interpret Ginny? Lee: No. What I really think is interesting to me is that the people who do it think of it as an extraordinary privilege to get to do it. It’s not like you’re trying to get rid of your kid. You’re thinking, I will scrape and save and borrow to send my kid overseas, because we think the American education is that important because my kid has to be a global child . Rosin: And do you see it that way? Lee: No. But you know what I do think? I think that what we don’t think about in America is the global contextualization of these parents’ decisions. We’re talking about people who have nothing, or very close to nothing, and they’re trying to figure out, How do I become an elite person? Not me, but my child become an elite person. Like, how do I give my kid a shot? And it’s usually through exams. So you’ll have somebody in China and in Korea, in India, doing these kinds of things, and you’re right. I mean, as a Western parent, it is really surprising. When you talk to the parents and you ask them what they went through, you really start to understand that this is their decision, and I have great sympathy for the parents who do this, as well as the kids. The kids are really confused, of course, because they’re just children. Rosin: Right. It’s so interesting to hear you talk about this, because I know that you exist in the tradition of social-realist novels of the 19th century, and there is an element of maybe social justice in that? Lee: Sure, sure. We’re from Queens! Rosin: We’re from Queens. We care about all the—we care about the underdogs. And I was wondering, is this like Upton Sinclair social justice? Like, I’m trying to expose the sort of crushing capitalist pressures that produce something like Ginny ? But that’s not really your tone, even though that’s, you know, a mode that you exist in. Your tone is a little more anthropologist. Lee: Yeah. I think you’re so smart to pick up on that, because there’s a part of me that wants to be the muckraker. But people don’t wanna read it. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: Yeah. Nobody wants that. Nobody wants the sermon. You know what people want? They want entertainment. And through entertainment and through drama, people will start to think, Oh, I really feel bad for this kid, Ginny. She’s 9 years old. She’s being parachuted . And all of a sudden, you become Ginny, ’cause that’s what fiction does. ’Cause you identify with somebody in the scene. You’re like, Well, how would that feel to be Ginny? And I’m actually saying, I want you to think about Ginny, but I also want you to think about the guardian. Asian parenting often becomes pathologized. It’s decontextualized. All we can see is the outcome, or we can see the data around it, but we don’t see the human interest. And as a matter of fact, if you were in the same situation, you might actually make the same decision. Rosin: What drew you to this subject after Pachinko ? Why education? Why did that become the thing that you thought was important to explore? Lee: So I’m gonna write this thing called Diaspora Quartet . All the books are not related in characters or plot, but they’re related by this idea of diaspora because I think diaspora is now the modern person’s permanent condition. Rosin: Interesting. What do you mean? Everybody? Lee: Everybody. Not just Koreans, everybody. So for example, environmental diaspora, right? So you don’t have any water in your city, in your town, and you have to move. You don’t have any more jobs in your town, so you have to move. If you wanna go get an education or you have to cross a border. And I’m saying that we are being scattered by modern society, so we have to study the subject. Like, I think we’ve gotta take it really seriously. So my entire novelistic work before I quit is going to be diaspora. The people that I look at are Koreans. That’s my lane. It’s a lane I really wanna be in. And after my first two books, I asked myself, What is the value that Koreans care about more than any other thing? Because, and I took it really based upon all my interviews. I’ve had thousands of interviews, and in every single one of them, they talk about education with this kind of controversial kind of take. They all care about the subject, but they have such different opinions on it that it always kinda took my breath away, because it was so not American. And that’s all I can say. It’s like, it was so unfamiliar to me, at the same time so familiar, because I heard it over and over again. Rosin: And how—what is it? How would you summarize it? Lee: That they care about it more than religion. They care more about it than money. They care more about it than status. Rosin: Like, it’s almost a faith. Lee: Yes. Yes. Rosin: Like, they believe it is a token to success, almost in a pachinko way of, like, If you get this token, everything will work out . Lee: Everything will work out, and also, it means so much to another person—like, if we learn, Oh, Hanna went to this school . I’m talking middle school. I’m not even talking about college here. Like, you went to this middle school. It means that you were in certain neighborhoods, and you’re, let’s say, the top student, ’cause they have that. They will remember the top student of a middle school. And consequently, that means something to your classmates who went to middle school with you. And I think the average American person would say, “That is insane.” ( Laughs .) Rosin: Right. Right. We don’t think of it as a belief in that way. Like, an absolute belief. Lee: Yeah. You know? So, I mean, and it wasn’t all the Koreans, but I would find Koreans who would say these things, and I thought, Huh, that’s so interesting . So I thought, Okay, I’m gonna write this book about education, and I’m going to connect it with diaspora , because it made a lot of sense to me, because they would always say, “I wanna go here to learn English for my kid.” And they would accept all these arrangements, like the parachute kid. Like the wild-geese phenomenon, which is when the father stays home, earns all the money, and the mom and the kid live somewhere else, like Australia, like the Philippines, in order to learn English. And people don’t really know that there are Koreans everywhere— Rosin: Yeah. Lee: —especially where English is spoken. And you wouldn’t—and it’s not so obvious why they go. Rosin: Yeah. So you’re both examining this idea and a little bit pushing back against this idea. Lee: I wanna figure it out, and then I also wanna be fair to it, ’cause there’s two things. One is I don’t think in America we talk enough about education. We’re not helping children get the skills they need to take care of themselves. That is— Rosin: Like, we’re failing in education. Lee: We’re failing. Rosin: We don’t worship it enough, or we don’t believe in it enough. Lee: Like, if we have Koreans who are doing things at this sort of intense rate, we are doing that almost as a nation. We’re falling behind. Rosin: In a too lackadaisical way. In fact, I would say the mythology that’s taken hold at this moment in America is the opposite. You’re wasting your time . Like, what you really should be doing is leaving your education and going to be an entrepreneur or a tech entrepreneur. Like, it’s like you’re a chump if you stick to the rote path. Lee: Well, also this whole chump-ness, the chump population, the fact that we can even call people chumps is so anti-intellectual. Like, which intellectual person would just say, “Oh, you’re a chump for getting a Ph.D.”? That you would study eight years to get a doctorate. Right? ’Cause the tech bros would be like, “You’re clearly a ding-dong, because I quit college.” Not all the tech bros, obviously, but I think that kind of thinking is—in Korea, if you have a Ph.D., that’s considered very honorable. By most people. Not everybody, but by many. Rosin: I was thinking of a specific scene in the novel. It’s this community gathering at a Christian church, and one of the main characters, whose name is Lion, is giving this big speech to all of the parents. Lion runs this very successful Hagwon business that caters to Korean immigrants in Los Angeles. And in his speech, he’s telling the parents, Will you please worry less about your kids’ grades and less about where they’re going to college, and more about their mental health? He’s essentially pushing back against all this intensity. It’s an interesting scene for a lot of reasons: (1) It doesn’t really work. Like, it just makes him sort of more valuable and ups the parents’ panic. And (2) it’s interesting because, like, he’s running a hagwon, so I’m not really sure how to under—it’s almost like the leaders of the AI companies who are like, Please restrain us . Like, he’s in charge of it, you know? So I was curious to hear you talk about that scene. Lee: You know, I met all these hagwon teachers who had been doing it for a long time, and the ones who have been doing it for a long time, the ones who are really good, they’re almost like teenage whisperers, because these young kids, they don’t feel heard. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: They’re told a lot of things, but they’re not heard. So when you have this magical person who went to the famous school that your parents want you to go to, and they really listen to you, and they ask you questions like, So why do you wanna go to college? Maybe it’s not a good time . And the kid’s like, What do you mean? I have a choice? And they get really excited. And I think when you can have access to what the kids are really thinking, it’s a very privileged position. And then I think these teachers start to really identify with the young people more, and they’re trying to help them. Because what ends up happening is some of these kids do go to these schools, and then after the first year, they literally just crash. And they’re also exhausted, especially in America. Because when you have 14 AP classes, no one should be doing that. Rosin: Okay, that’s actually very helpful because the hagwon where a lot of the action takes place, the one run by Lion, is essentially—what it stands for is not a bucking of the system or a resistance. What it stands for is connection. Like, it’s a place where it’s an idealized form of tutoring and education, like, almost a connection between teacher and student. I have no idea if that exists or is common among hagwons, but that’s what novelistically it represents. Lee: I saw hagwon teachers. Overwhelmingly, they’re pretty decent people. But I have met hagwon teachers who do bad things, who cheat. Rosin: Who help the children cheat. Like they teach them bad values. Lee: Yeah, or they write the college essays. They just take the parents’ money, and they churn these things out, and they also—the worst thing I think they do by cheating is by telling the kids, “This is the way the world works. So you carry on, and you keep doing this.” Rosin: Right. So it makes them cynical. Lee: Oh, the young people right now are so cynical in a way that you and I are like innocent, so innocent at that age, because we did not know. I shouldn’t speak for you, Hanna, but most people that I knew at Bronx Science, we did not really understand a lot of things. Like, I didn’t know about legacies, for example. I didn’t know about having a famous parent. Like, I didn’t know about the sports track of how you get into school, especially at Bronx Science. There are so many things I didn’t know, and I think that when you figure out, actually, if there are 1,200 seats in a class for that college, really there are about 400 left for the general population. And of that, that needs to be divided among a global constituency. Rosin: Now that you do know all these things, you did go to elite colleges. Lee: I did. Yeah. Rosin: So when you look back, I mean, you went to some of the most prestigious universities, Yale and Georgetown. Did writing this book make you think differently about your experience in elite academia? Lee: Well, I think that when I went to these elite spaces, except for Bronx Science, where I really felt normal and happy—it’s New York, and it’s just other kids from the boroughs. And also, not that much was expected of me. Like, I didn’t have a lot of pressure at home to study and to become something. Rosin: Because your parents were not the so-called tiger parents. Lee: No. My mother’s very laissez-faire, ’cause she went to a very prestigious school in Korea, and she’s a music person, and her attitude is, “If you have the brains and you squander it, that’s on you.” Rosin: That’s nice. There’s freedom in that. Lee: There’s a lot of freedom in it, and there’s three of us. So her attitude is, well, you know, again, I was considered sort of the slower of the pack. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: So then I really, I just, I was left to sort of read the free books and eventually find my way. And I think when I went to college, I met all these kids who were so polished and sophisticated and suave, and they were so well traveled. They just knew things that I just didn’t know, and I remember feeling like, Oh, I don’t know that. I really don’t know that, and I’ve never been there, and I don’t know how to pronounce that . Like, there were so many things I had read but I didn’t know how to say. [ Music ] Rosin: After the break, more on Min Jin Lee’s new novel, American Hagwon , and why she sees herself as a moral novelist. [ Break ] Rosin: The novel is bookended by two financial catastrophes: the 1997 IMF crisis in South Korea and the 2008 subprime-mortgage crisis in the U.S. Why was it important for you to set it in this time period? What kind of pressure, extra pressure does that create? Lee: Well, I wanna talk about now. I mean, I write social novels, and I think one of the things that we don’t wanna do is: We don’t wanna recognize the villains in our lives, because they’re not legible to us. Like, a financial crisis—we don’t understand how much damage it does to all of us all the time, because we don’t wanna understand the subjects. Rosin: I see. So it’s easy to understand, like, a bad parent who ships—that’s very concrete. Lee: Yes, yes. Rosin: Yes, I see. Lee: Yeah. A bad parent, a war. Rosin: Yes. Lee: The other country. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Right? A religious group that you don’t like. That’s very easy to say, Oh, it’s them. It’s not me . A financial crisis? We all actually participate in it. And we don’t wanna be responsible for learning about it. And, again, that’s education. I actually think that if we had personal-finance classes, it would make a humongous difference in the way America runs. Rosin: Just as in Pachinko , because of this financial crisis and other reasons, there are wild swings to family fortunes. What is interesting to you about putting your characters through that kind of suffering? What is important to learn about a family, or is that a way of testing people or evoking certain things? Lee: Well, it’s actually what happens to all of us. Somebody loses a job. When one parent loses a job or is, as we say, reduced , you wake up, you open your computer, and you get an email saying, Your division is gone . That’s America now. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: How does that affect your family? Especially if the parent is, let’s say, 47 or 52. It’s really difficult to start again— Rosin: Yeah. Lee: —at this age. And I wanted to show that happening to my characters because that’s what’s happening to us now. Rosin: Now, if that situation happens, there are a lot of directions: The family could break apart. People could get angry, violent. The family you feature, what’s remarkable about them is they almost immediately choose to sacrifice for each other. The father goes from corporate world to working in a fish-fry restaurant. The daughter, who’s really, really smart, decides, Oh, I’m gonna work and put my brothers through school . So it’s a lot of sacrifice. What’s interesting to you about sacrifice? Lee: Well, when I interviewed all these different families around the world about their education, especially the ones that lost everything in the IMF crisis, the ones who actually succeeded, the only survival strategy that worked was sacrifice and sequencing. Rosin: What do you mean? Is it sacrifice within the family context? Lee: Yeah. Somebody had to give. Not everybody’s gonna get what they want. Rosin: Uh-huh. Lee: And it may seem pretty logical and obvious, but if everybody tries to get what they want, then the entire unit breaks apart. Rosin: Yeah. I was wondering if you were working through the Korean concept or even a Christian concept of sacrifice. Lee: You know, it’s actually, I think there are religious aspects of it that I think are valuable, and it’s shared cross-culturally by families who have faith in a religion, but also it was just the only thing that’s gonna work, because there’s limited resources and limited time. So even if, take religion away, I think even economists would understand that sequencing is sometimes the only choice. Like, if you only have $100, and $40 is all you could spend for education, and you have, let’s say, three kids, you can’t do it for all the kids. Rosin: It’s funny, when you talk about some of these things or these decisions, you talk about the analytical part of them and less about the sort of spiritual, philosophical part of it. Like, in the book, the way sacrifice happens—I mean, there’s a lot of morality. Would you agree with that, that there is— Lee: I’m definitely a moral writer. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: I’m definitely a moral novelist. I mean, in the same way all the writers that I love are moral novelists. Actually, you know why? Because, actually, I think most people are desperate for morality. ( Laughs .) Rosin: And what do you mean by “morality”? ’Cause there’s one surface-level reading, which is that in this novel, family is really important and central, holds people together, and people really sacrifice for their families. And the one person who does things which are very patently, say, un-Christian—lie, steal, seduce married men—really gets her comeuppance. So that’s almost a traditional kind of morality. But maybe that’s not what you mean by morality. Lee: No. That’s actually just law. I mean, I was a former lawyer. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Yeah. Lee: So I have seen people who behave this way get in trouble. I’ve talked to a lot of white-collar-criminal lawyers. So it’s really interesting. So you can argue that in this current climate, that we should celebrate the antihero. We could, right? Rosin: And I would say a lot of Korean movies about inequality, at least the ones that are popular here, are very antihero, like Squid Game . I mean, they’re brutal and they don’t have any traditional morality. They definitely celebrate the antihero. Lee: Right. But so I know the director and the writer of that show, for example, and when we talk about politics, he’s a very moral person. Rosin: Interesting. Lee: I mean, the reason why you show that in a satirical way is because you’re so outraged by the inequality. I think Koreans are really outraged by unfairness. Like, if you wanna have a scandal in Korea as a politician, your kid cheats on something and you let it go, that actually becomes a national scandal. If your wife accepts a handbag and she shouldn’t have, that’s corruption. Rosin: That’s interesting, ’cause right now there’s sort of beginning to be a call for Democrats not to just talk about affordability, but to talk about how unfair things are. You know, to sort of add a kind of element of injustice and morality to what’s happening, which we see in data centers. It hasn’t quite percolated into the political language quite yet, but it’s there. When you said people are desperate for morality, what is in your head? What are you thinking about? Lee: Well, when I take the temperature of America right now with the people that I meet, people are really upset about the fact that we’re all so cynical, including children. Nobody believes in anything. And we think that terrible things are happening, and nobody’s being held accountable. Yet regular middle-class people still have to pay their bills, and we can’t ask questions why. Gas prices are going up. Egg prices are going up. The rent’s going up. There’s no house to buy. The interest rates are going up. So this affordability crisis is a lot about, Hey, this is not fair , because some people who have assets are doing great, ’cause the stock market, despite all these things, is artificially inflated, and it’s doing great. But if you’re the chump who doesn’t have assets, you’re really upset. Again, fairness. Rosin: Yeah. Lee: You know, I think most people really see themselves as decent. That’s the other thing. ’Cause I’ve interviewed a lot of people who do some crazy bad things, illegal things. And they always have a reason why. And they’ll say things like, I did it for my family. I did it for my mother . I did it for X, Y, Z . And you’re kind of going like, But it’s illegal . But they have a reason. And so when I listen to them, I go, Okay, well, most people really believe that they’re pretty decent . And then I meet people who are really trying to do the right thing with almost nothing. That always stuns me. Rosin: Yeah. So you’ve talked a little bit about the quartet here. The fourth book is gonna be called the Marshall Plan . It’s always terrible to ask someone: How’s it going? ( Laughs .) Lee: ( Laughs .) Rosin: I’m not even gonna ask. Lee: I started. Rosin: Oh, you did? Congratulations. Lee: Thank you. Rosin: Can you just talk a little bit about what you’re exploring in the Marshall Plan ? Lee: So I think that the Marshall Plan is probably the smartest, most moral thing America did. Rosin: Let’s just say what it is. Lee: Sure. Rosin: It’s the 1948 U.S. initiative to help with economic recovery in Europe after World War II. How’s that as a summary? Lee: Very, very. That’s— Rosin: Thank you. Lee: A+. Rosin: Okay. Lee: And the reason why that’s quite astonishing is because we could have taken the tack, Germany, you did something beyond evil. You should be punished. You should just suffer , right? But I think that people were aware that that suffering during World War I and the economic terms, which caused inflation and which caused this demagogue to become powerful, and then he scapegoated a minority, maybe we don’t wanna do that again. And by rebuilding—and rebuilding by giving money to Europe—all of us benefited, America and Europe. So it’s this thing that I think we always turn to in saying, We could do that . Rosin: Yeah. Lee: Why don’t we do that again? Why do we always like hurting people? I’m writing something called, Marshall Plan , not the Marshall Plan. And it’s about this idea of remittances and reconstruction. So all these Koreans left Korea in the ’60s and ’70s, and they went to Germany to work as miners and nurses, about 20,000 of them. And they sent their deutsche marks back to South Korea to help rebuild the country. And then also, many Koreans went to Europe and became artists and learned more about the arts in Europe: singers, violinists, filmmakers, photographers. And then also, many women married GIs and went to America, and they sent money back to South Korea. I’m interested in this idea of remittances. Rosin: I’m seeing—as you’re talking, I think I’m getting a better sense because it’s not a quartet in that we’re following the same characters over time, but you are thinking very hard about the world as it is, kind of different ways that it could be. Lee: Yes. Rosin: And morality in a sort of complex way, because it’s a morality that is constrained and exists in a very realistic world. Like, a world in which no one’s really dealt a fair hand, in which bad things happen, and particularly to people who don’t have that much power. Lee: Yeah. Rosin: You know? Lee: No, you’re getting it. You’re really getting it. And it’s so important to me, because I’m not that interested in pointing out problems. I’m trying to figure out what works, and what has worked for people who have very little. Because all I hear all the time is that the world is burning down. And I’m thinking, like, This is not what we tell college students or teenagers. It’s not something that we tell middle-aged people . ( Laughs .) Rosin: You mean because it’s not inspiring? Lee: Because (1) it’s also not true. It’s not true. If you look at the history of the world, things are horrible now, but they’re also—it was horrible then. And in some ways, significantly more horrible then. For women, right? All the illnesses that we’ve cured since then. And I keep thinking, Well, how did all of our ancestors deal with these horrific problems of just foolishness and hatred? All of it . And we need to figure something out, and we need to remember, because I know that this, like, perpetual state of fear and anxiety is not something that we can—like, we can’t do this. We have to have another story. [ Music ] Rosin: This is so good because I think a lot of people in this moment in American history take the path of avoidance or distraction. And you are essentially writing or speaking an intellectual’s guide to a happy life. Like, a high-information guide to a happy life. So I appreciate it. Well, Min, thank you so much for joining me. And congratulations. Lee: Well, Hanna, now that I know that we’re twins. ( Laughs .) Rosin: Yeah. I know, I kinda wish I’d gone to Bronx Science, you know? [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Yvonne Kim fact-checked. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: US: Nebraskans Losing Coverage as Medicaid Changes
items.description: Nebraska’s efforts to implement new, federally mandated work requirements for Medicaid underscore fears that millions of people will experience avoidable barriers to healthcare coverage.Federal authorities could have chosen to blunt the impact of the federal legislation’s Medicaid cuts. Instead, they added even more convoluted requirements that will deprive people of health care they are entitled to.Nebraska is the canary in the coal mine for issues that most states will face when they begin implementing these work requirements. As they do, they should make sure red tape doesn’t strip people of health care. (Washington, DC) – Nebraska’s efforts to implement new, federally mandated work requirements for Medicaid underscore fears that millions of people will experience avoidable barriers to healthcare coverage, Human Rights Watch, Oxfam America, and Nebraska Appleseed said today. On May 1, 2026, Nebraska became the first state to implement work requirements for Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people with low- or no-income, as part of public spending cuts mandated by the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which also extended and deepened tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefit high-income households and corporations. These new rules will require most adults without dependents to document at least 80 hours per month of work, education, or other approved activities to maintain Medicaid coverage. States must implement the requirements by January 1, 2027, though they may do so sooner, as Nebraska has. “Nebraska is the canary in the coal mine for issues that most states will face when they begin implementing these work requirements,” said Matt McConnell, US researcher on economic, social, and cultural rights at Human Rights Watch. “As they do, they should make sure red tape doesn’t strip people of health care.” Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America in August and September interviewed a dozen Nebraskans with personal or professional experience with Medicaid and a public employee involved in the process. People interviewed said that the state’s rollout of new work requirements increased administrative burdens and risked disruptions in access to health care following the rushed implementation of these federal requirements. Data suggests that large numbers of people are already losing coverage in Nebraska because of the work requirements. Eli McCreary, age 64 at the time, said he lost his Medicaid coverage while undergoing treatment for kidney cancer and multiple chronic health conditions. He said a representative of the health plan that managed his Medicaid coverage informed him he lost access because he was not working, even though he is unable to work due to his condition. “If I could work, I would work,” he said. “But I can’t…. I can’t walk around. I mean, I can’t breathe. I can’t walk very far.” The sudden lapse in coverage disrupted his planned care. “I was supposed to go see the cancer specialist here…. And that date was canceled, so I couldn’t. I had to wait until I got insurance again to even come back out here.... Everything was delayed.” A Medicaid eligibility worker from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services said that poor training, vague and inconsistent guidance, and technical issues, including unprepared software systems, had caused stress and uncertainty for applicants and for state employees. “We just sometimes don’t know what we’re doing,” the worker said, describing the rollout as rushed and confusing. “I wish the people who make policies knew what they were doing.” The OBBBA, which became law in July 2025, imposed new eligibility criteria on the nearly 20 million adults without dependents in the 40 states and the District of Columbia who rely on expanded Medicaid coverage under the Affordable Care Act. Nebraska expanded coverage through a ballot initiative in 2018. Adults in this expansion population will be required to prove that they either satisfy these new work requirements or qualify for a statutory exemption, including for caregivers of young children, pregnant people, certain people with disabilities, and those deemed medically frail. States may also choose to offer short-term hardship exceptions for certain individuals, such as those in counties with a federally declared emergency or disaster. The Urban Institute estimated that between 3 and 7 million people in the United States could lose Medicaid coverage by 2028 because of these new requirements. The Congressional Budget Office, a nonpartisan government research agency, estimated that work requirements would increase the number of uninsured people in the United States by 4.8 million by 2034. Nebraska Appleseed, a Lincoln-based nonprofit advocacy organization, has repeatedly requested data from the state regarding its implementation of these requirements. On September 29, 2026, Nebraska publicly released initial figures showing that over 1,000 people lost or were denied Medicaid coverage under the new requirements between May and August of this year. The number of people affected is likely to grow significantly over the coming months as state officials review enrollees’ eligibility on a rolling basis. “Getting data from the state about how many people are losing coverage and why shouldn’t be like pulling teeth,” said Sarah Maresh, healthcare access program director at Nebraska Appleseed. “Nebraskans deserve access to this information. You can’t fix problems you refuse to measure.” In May, Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America warned that millions of people were at risk of losing coverage due to the work requirements. In a joint letter to the US Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the organizations urged federal authorities to issue guidance for states that would help prevent these new federal requirements from causing harmful and unnecessary Medicaid denials and terminations. But CMS issued binding guidance on June 1 that will require burdensome case-by-case assessments. “Federal authorities could have chosen to blunt the impact of the OBBBA’s inequality-fueling Medicaid cuts,” said Jackson Gandour, senior economic justice policy adviser at Oxfam America. “Instead, they added even more convoluted requirements that will deprive people of the health care they are entitled to.” Under international human rights law, everyone has the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. Medicaid eligibility requirements already exclude people who earn too much to meet extremely low-income eligibility limits but not enough to afford private health insurance. Complex work reporting requirements may exclude millions more, undermining their rights to health, social security, and an adequate standard of living. Because the rules largely affect people with low incomes, these losses may also deepen inequality, the organizations said. Officials in Nebraska and other states preparing to implement the work requirement provisions should identify ways to reduce administrative burdens and simplify eligibility assessments. Officials should also take steps to strengthen existing exemptions; improve communication about, and understanding of, who is subject to work requirements and who is exempt; and enhance transparency by regularly publishing data on application denials, coverage terminations, appeals, reinstatements, and the reasons underlying these decisions. “Work requirements are a solution in search of a problem,” McConnell said. “The truth is that they make life harder for people who are already working or can’t work.” Widespread Confusion; Risk of Disrupted Care People currently on Medicaid expressed confusion about whether work requirements or relevant exemptions applied to them, and what steps they needed to take to maintain coverage. “I got a letter early in January stating that the work requirements were coming, and then basically, that’s it,” said Schmeeka Simpson, a 44-year-old community organizer in Omaha and mother of three. She said she received a letter informing her that she was approved for Medicaid in August, but with no explanation for how Nebraska determined she complied with the work requirements. “I’m like ‘great, that’s wonderful,’ but I don't know how they came to those conclusions.” Due to the lack of clarity, Simpson said, it is difficult to know how to maintain Medicaid eligibility. “Who, what, when, where, why, and how hasn’t been answered…. These are life and death situations for people. This is not just politics.” Melissa Craig, a single mother in Omaha who relies on Medicaid, said she only learned that she qualified for an exemption to work requirements shortly before they went into effect: “It is very stressful for me on a day-to-day basis about what my future and my son’s future looks like. Staying on top of it is a full-time job.” Megan Word, government relations director covering Nebraska and Kansas for American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), said “The workers can’t even quickly identify whether somebody is on the expansion population or not.” She said even Medicaid eligibility workers may be unaware of whether someone will be subject to work requirements. “The biggest concern is the administrative burden that is going to be placed on ... the patient,” said Amy Behnke, who leads the Health Center Association of Nebraska, which represents the seven healthcare providers operating federally qualified health centers in Nebraska. She said: “Prior to Medicaid expansion, our health centers had a 50 percent uninsured rate, and now we’re down to about a third. So, expansion has been incredibly significant to our health centers and to their patients … [But] often what we see with patients is that … they’re working sometimes multiple jobs, they’re taking care of their families, they’re figuring out how to put food on their table. And so, any time you ask somebody to take one more step when it comes to verifying their health insurance, the higher the likelihood is that something is going to fall through the cracks.” She described a recent case at one of the centers she represents. A pregnant woman arrived for a prenatal appointment and learned she no longer had Medicaid coverage, despite being exempt from work requirements. Eventually staff determined that state officials had overlooked a box indicating she was pregnant and the woman was able to regain Medicaid coverage, but it took multiple calls and she had to reschedule appointments. “This never should have been an issue,” Behnke said. Confusion surrounding work requirements may also discourage otherwise eligible people from applying for Medicaid coverage. “I had three different patients outright tell me, ‘What’s the point of enrolling? I’m not employed,’” said a licensed social worker based in Omaha who like some others spoke on condition of anonymity. She stressed that working with a social worker was essential to getting these people to apply. “It really, in our experience, becomes a game of how connected you are to a caseworker who can write these accommodations or write these letters and verify your status. And it really just becomes, just kind of a dice roll of privilege, unfortunately.” This confusion may already be causing disruptions in care. McCreary, the Omaha man who lost coverage while undergoing cancer treatment, learned that he had lost Medicaid coverage from his healthcare providers. “Unless you’re going to self-pay, we can’t take you, because your insurance canceled out,” he said, describing his conversation with hospital staff. “I had to cancel all of my appointments.” He said that when he contacted the managed care organization that administered his Medicaid coverage, he was informed that he had lost coverage because he was not working. “They said, you’re not working. I can’t really do anything for you.” Administrative Capacity and Perverse Incentives Implementing these work requirements involves creating new administrative processes within state agencies overseeing Medicaid, as well as training for the public employees who administer them, the organizations said. The federal law also requires all states, starting in January 2027, to increase the frequency of eligibility redeterminations from once per year, as required by the federal Affordable Care Act, to every six months. While this will effectively double the number of eligibility determinations the department must process each year, staffing is not keeping up with the increased workload. In the December 2025 news conference to announce that Nebraska would be the first state to implement work requirements under the OBBBA, Governor Jim Pillen said that no extra staff would be hired to help track work requirements. In July, Nebraska instituted a hiring freeze for state agencies including the health department citing a state budget shortfall that has been worsened by a 2023 law that nearly halved Nebraska’s tax rate for the highest earners. One Medicaid eligibility worker said that capacity issues, along with internal bureaucratic incentives, exacerbate the risk that eligible people will be denied coverage. They said chronic understaffing and pressure to clear cases is compounded by confusion and a lack of adequate training around the eligibility changes: “We just sometimes don’t know what we are doing … and then you have [Medicaid applicants] coming in, understandably they’re upset.” They said staff had recently been required to revisit some cases because supervisors had relayed incorrect information. “The supervisors were told something wrong and told us something wrong and now we’re having to go back and fix all these cases.” The worker said they face pressure to increase the number of cases closed. “You have to get your numbers up,” the worker said, relaying the message they and other staff regularly get from managers. “That’s really messed up because denials are the easiest.” This prioritizes speed over accuracy, the worker said, incentivizing staff to rapidly deny applications if there is any cause and disincentivizing staff from spending the time necessary to correct apparent errors, omissions, or inquiring more about potential pathways to coverage through existing exemptions. “All of that work that you do to try to verify, it doesn’t count. So, it looks like you did nothing,” the worker said. “All I think about is numbers and getting it done. I get so anxious and nervous.” Rushed and Unclear Implementation In Nebraska’s rush to be the first state to implement the work requirements, it developed eligibility criteria before official federal guidance was issued. The result has been a mismatch between the state and federal eligibility rules. “Nebraska went live with their work requirement implementation on May 1 and the Feds published their [mandatory guidance] on June 1,” said Megan Word of the ACS CAN. “[Nebraska] did not pause. They did not say, ‘Wait a minute … we need to review the differences,’ because there were many.” She said before the federal government issued mandatory guidance in June, through the Interim Final Rule, Nebraska had created a list of medical codes for diagnoses that might automatically satisfy the “medically frail” exemption to work requirements written into the OBBBA. “If you can find one of those medical conditions on the list, then theoretically, you should be eligible for an exemption,” Word said. However, this was inconsistent with the federal rule. Under that rule, a diagnosis such as cancer does not automatically establish an exemption, leaving many people who are unable to work because of their health unsure of whether they remain eligible for Medicaid. Instead, the federal rule defines “medically frail” as a “physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition [that] significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply” with work requirements. “The Interim Final Rule makes it harder for patients to obtain this exemption,” Word said, because it puts the burden of proving one’s inability to work on enrollees, while also requiring a case-by-case review from implementing agencies. “That will involve some sort of independent verification, a process that no one really understands at this point.” For the time being, Nebraska is allowing people to submit a declaration—“self-attest”—that they are “medically frail” without having to provide additional supporting documentation. Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America recommended that federal authorities should help enable self-attestation in its May letter. Although the rules published in June allowed states to accept self-attestation for an exemption from work requirements, it only allows states to do so until January 2028, after which states will only be allowed to accept self-attestation when documentation is not “reasonably available.” In practice, both a lack of awareness regarding the availability of these exemptions and a broad misunderstanding about who may be eligible for them undermines the temporary availability of self-attestation, the groups found. People who may be unable to work because of their health must also juggle bureaucratic hurdles to prove their eligibility, frequently while undergoing sometimes intensive medical treatment. According to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organization, more than 6 out of every 10 people under age 65 on Medicaid are already working full or part time. About 3 out of 10 are not working because of caregiving responsibilities, disability, or illness, or because they are attending school. Fewer than 1 in 10 are unemployed for another reason, including retirement or the inability to find work. “Why are you putting in work requirements when the majority of people who rely on Medicaid are already working anyway?” Word said. Lessons from Georgia Human Rights Watch and Oxfam America’s joint research in the state of Georgia—which in 2023 expanded Medicaid coverage to adults without dependents but conditioned eligibility on meeting work requirements similar to those in OBBBA—indicate that work requirements compound existing barriers to accessing health care. According to data provided by the state to the Georgia Budget & Policy Institute, a nonprofit advocacy organization, over 100,000 people are estimated to be eligible for Georgia’s Medicaid expansion, but as of August 2026, only 20,321 were enrolled. According to the latest data published by the state of Georgia, about half of the 17,638 denials for their Medicaid expansion program between October 2024 and September 2025 were due to a failure to either meet or verify compliance with work requirements. Lack of Transparency Because Nebraska has been slow to release data on the impact of work requirements on Medicaid enrollment, advocates have struggled to assess the impacts of these policies. “We’re flying blind,” Behnke said. Without detailed data, health centers cannot identify where patients are losing coverage or adjust outreach strategies effectively. OBBBA’s Disproportionate Impact on Low-Income Households The addition of work requirements to Medicaid was among a series of provisions in OBBBA that reduced federal spending on public services and programs, including through restrictive eligibility and reporting requirements. These reductions were designed in part to offset tax cuts that disproportionately benefit high-income households and corporations. The nonpartisan Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation found that the top 0.1 percent of earners will receive an average tax cut of $311,000 in 2027 because of the OBBBA, while taxes will increase for the lowest-income households. The Congressional Budget Office found that the OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements will reduce federal spending by $326 billion over the next decade. Meanwhile, the total cost of the OBBBA’s tax breaks for corporations and the wealthiest 1 percent of households is estimated at around $2 trillion.

items.title: 'Off-the-record talks' between PTI and govt ongoing: Rana Sanaullah
items.description: Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Thursday that the federal government and PTI were engaged in “off-the-record talks” regarding PTI’s planned protest on October 4. Sanaullah made the remarks while appearing in Geo News ’ morning show “Geo Pakistan”. Sanaullah said that the decision on the proposed march rested with PTI’s senior leadership, “with whom off-the-record consultation is ongoing”. “So let us see, even if they do not postpone it, we have arrangements in place to stop them,” Sanaullah warned. He likened the PTI’s march to a “provincial government attacking the capital” in an apparent reference to the PTI-led government in KP. “If a political party or a private organisation stages a protest, [..] but for a government to attack [..] it cannot be tolerated under any circumstances,” he held. “The law will be enacted in full force, and they (PTI) will be barred from entering Islamabad,” he added. Responding to a question about governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sanaullah on Thursday said that the option was “on the table”. Sanaullah further clarified that the federal government was in talks with coalition parties about imposing governor’s rule in KP. He added that the final decision rested upon the federal government and the Senate, adding that it would only come into effect with parliament’s approval. Sanaullah alleged that the KP CM had not been performing his functions as the province’s chief executive. “For the past two months, he has not done anything, nothing about development or counter-terrorism efforts or for the welfare of people [..] in fact, all he has done is talk about marching to Islamabad and toppling the federal government. “They want to take ladders to Islamabad to secure the release of a certain someone,” he added. Sanaullah reiterated that if a province is “engaged in such illegal and unconstitutional activities, then the Centre has the right to declare emergency or governor rule and assume power”. The Oct 4 march — which the PTI has announced as part of its nationwide protest to demand the release of its founder, Imran Khan — remains a major bone of contention between the government and the main opposition party, with both taking entrenched positions. Originally scheduled for Sept 27, the march was postponed to Oct 4 last week. On its part, the government has been adamant that it would not allow the party to block roads and disrupt routine life. To back their resolve, authorities had taken extraordinary security measures to ens­ure that the proposed march never made it to the capital, including blocking bridges, roads and motorways leading to the twin cities. It has also threatened to send the PTI government in KP packing by imposing governor’s rule or an emergency if the provincial leadership does not withdraw its plan to march on Islamabad on Oct 4 . Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said on Wednesday that the federal government was “ seriously considering ” imposing an emergency in KP.

items.description: The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has urged Nigerians to keep the hope alive in spite of the present challenges, saying the future of Nigeria is bright. PDP National Publicity Secretary Mr Jungudo Mohammed stated this in a statement issued by the party to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary on Thursday in Abuja. Mohammed said that the PDP acknowledged that, as a nation and as a people, Nigeria and Nigerians were not yet where they aspired to be; however, they must not despair. “The future of Nigeria remains bright, and our collective hope must remain stronger than our present challenges. “Nigeria is a blessed nation, endowed with enormous human and natural resources. “Let us harness these resources, alongside our rich ethnic, cultural and religious diversity, into an instrument of unity, creativity and national progress,” he said. Mohammed called on all Nigerians to continue to preach peace, unity and national cohesion. He also called on leaders and followers alike to remain patriotic, reject violence and corruption, and always place the interests of Nigeria above personal and sectional considerations. “Above all, let us build a nation where our young people can dream, aspire and look to the future with confidence and hope,” he said. The national publicity secretary pledged the PDP’s continued commitment to democracy, good governance and the welfare of the Nigerian people. “We are poised to provide the alternative platform and leadership needed to help Nigeria realise her full potential and achieve the dreams and aspirations of her citizens. “As we celebrate our nation, let us honour the sacrifices of our founding fathers and all those who have contributed to our national development, and ensure that the labour of our heroes past shall not be in vain. “Together, let us renew our commitment to building a better Nigeria and restoring hope for the younger generations. “Nigeria has what it takes to rise! Nigeria shall be great!” Mohammed said. (NAN) The post Nigeria ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‌⁠⁠‍‌​​‍‌‌​at 66: Our hope must remain alive – PDP appeared first on Vanguard News .
