The Flailing President
items.description: T he White House’s South Lawn was prepared just so: A full honor guard, complete with American and Chinese flags, stood at attention. The new White House helipad, made of four-inch-thick black-and-white California granite, seemed to gleam. President Trump appeared pleased—but something was missing. Where were the TV cameras? For a president who needs media attention like he needs oxygen, this was an unacceptable development ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s welcome ceremony last week. Trump whirled around to his aides and demanded they fix it, and a staffer raced to the briefing room to ask ABC News whether it would film the arrival, two people familiar with the exchange told me on the condition of anonymity, given the private nature of the conversations. But the answer was no: The networks were boycotting participation in the TV-pool rotation in solidarity with CNN, which Trump had banned from the White House, along with two other media outlets, days before. No major U.S. television network recorded Trump’s over-the-top greeting for Xi, and the news channels refused to display images taken by the White House or any other outlet, American or Chinese. Trump did not get to show off his extravaganza. And he had only himself to blame. At the risk of understatement, Trump has never been one to think all that many moves ahead. But his impulsive decision to ban media outlets spawned unintended consequences that derailed his own plans. Again. That’s been a real theme for much of this year: Many of Trump’s actions—quite a few impetuous and ill-considered—have only hurt him and his fellow Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. He was elected two years ago to drive down prices, but his tariffs have done the opposite, and a recent reignited trade war with Canada has hurt Republican candidates whose state shares a border with our neighbor to the north. His war of choice in Iran continues to sputter along, leaving gas prices elevated as Trump threatens annihilation one day and offers negotiation the next. He insists on championing AI while the public has swiftly turned on it. And he’s obsessed with vanity projects—including, yes, that helipaid that cost at least $5 million—even as polls suggest that many Americans feel that he is out of touch with the Everyman he once claimed to represent. The numbers are bad: Trump’s approval rating dropped to 37 percent in a new Wall Street Journal poll this week, marking the lowest rating in that poll since 1990 for an incumbent president heading into a midterm election. He’s even lower in other polls. The president, the most dominant figure in the GOP in generations, will soon hit the campaign trail for his party—but he is beginning in deep-red states, an eyebrow-raising bit of scheduling that suggests acknowledgment of his weak political standing. More and more Republicans are starting to worry about a blue wave, one that seems certain to secure the House for Democrats but could very well, in an outcome unthinkable even a few months ago, yield a Democratic Senate as well. With barely a month until Election Day, and with early voting already under way in a number of states, Trump and his party are flailing. A Trump rally has been the signature political event of the past decade of American politics. The president considered forever walking away from them after his final one during the 2024 campaign, but he has been talked into reviving them now and then at a smaller scale and with heavy security. He held only a handful last year and, despite aides promising that he’d barnstorm the country with more frequency in 2026, rallies have still been rare; in September, he held just one (in North Carolina). He’s traveled domestically far less this term, distancing himself from the concerns of his voters. But with October and the stretch run of the midterm campaigns now here, Trump seems set to gas up Air Force One. Trump will begin with visits to two GOP strongholds (Oklahoma today, Alabama tomorrow) before then journeying on Saturday to Ohio, a state he won three times but where polls show Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted trailing his Democratic opponent, former Senator Sherrod Brown . Ohio is not the only reliably red state that now seems to have a Senate seat up for grabs: Iowa, Texas, Alaska, Kansas, and maybe even Nebraska (where Trump will travel next week) are all now in play. Earlier this year, the 2026 Senate map looked foreboding for Democrats; now strategists from both parties view control as a toss-up. Matthew Bartlett, a GOP strategist who worked in the first Trump administration but quit after the January 6 Capitol riot, told me that the president hasn’t given Republicans anything to run on, saying they have “no results to point to, no agenda to promise either.” And he said that many in the party feel that the bottom is dropping out and a wipeout could be coming. “Many recent elections have broken late, and hard, and often in one direction only,” Bartlett told me. “Among Republicans there is little hope that things get better before Election Day, but grave concern they may get worse.” Despite the challenges facing Republicans across the country, neither Senate race in Alabama or Oklahoma seems particularly close (at least for now). So why is Trump going there? For any president, even an unpopular one, his most valuable resource is his time—and heading to those deep-red states comes at the expense of a potential stop in a swing district (though the stop in southern Oklahoma does bleed into a Texas media market). The answer might be surprisingly simple: ego. “The president knows he is still going to get big, adoring crowds there,” one close outside adviser told me. Plus, there has been some debate in GOP circles as to whether or not a Trump visit would actually help in some battlegrounds; several Republicans in tight races are weighing whether to request a presidential visit, party strategists have told me. Two candidates, Susan Collins of Maine and John Sununu of New Hampshire, have already said no , and others have refused to commit. Another GOP strategist familiar with the president’s travel plans insisted to me that Trump will travel frequently and help boost turnout for Republican candidates, but they allowed that polling may suggest states that Trump should avoid. The White House downplayed any internal GOP concerns. The spokesperson Davis Ingle told me in a statement that “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” [ Read: The Republicans are bolting from Trump ] Yet there have been signs of Republicans distancing themselves from Trump on more issues, including immigration enforcement and ending the war in Iran. But that unpopular conflict may shadow the party for the foreseeable future : Many diplomats from the Middle East who attended the United Nations General Assembly last week privately feel that the war will, in stops and starts, likely continue well into next year and potentially throughout the rest of Trump’s term, threatening to drag down Republicans’ political fortunes for multiple elections. T rump has lurched from one distraction to another—Renaming Lake Ontario! Offering $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans win in November!—but he has yet to shift the electorate’s dim view of his presidency. He’s still pushing claims of election fraud, even though few Republican candidates have joined in. He even authorized the Department of Homeland Security to use taxpayer money to pay for what is, in essence, a Trump campaign ad despite prohibitions on using federal funds for propaganda. Trump took this provocative step while sitting on a massive campaign war chest, and many Republicans groaned at yet another unnecessary controversy. “I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, told reporters this week. The weekend before that, Trump abruptly banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds without telling many of his senior aides (some of whom, on a Friday afternoon, had already left for the weekend). He was reportedly frustrated by some of the coverage that his close aide Natalie Harp had shown him. A few days later, a federal judge ordered that the three media organizations be allowed to return to the White House complex. Even then, the president’s aides found ways to temporarily block them from certain events—and trigger alarms that Trump was beginning to defy court orders. But some of the president’s advisers told me they saw the ban as counterproductive and could, as it did with the Xi visit, deprive Trump of some of the media coverage he craves. That moment with China’s leader underscored what is arguably Trump’s biggest problem: He has lost touch with what Americans actually care about. The Xi summit was a cornucopia of warning signs for worried Republicans. It came amid a national discourse about the dangers of artificial intelligence, which included a push from industry leaders for additional safeguards on a fast-growing technology that, some insiders have warned, could wipe out humanity. But Trump’s been fixated on how AI has propped up the stock market and some sectors of the economy, and he has refused to slow down its growth . His one nod to how poorly AI is being perceived: He suggested it be renamed “super intelligence,” or SI. [ Read: The deferential president ] The entire decadent spectacle seemed out of step with a country deep in an affordability crisis. The black-tie guest list was dotted with billionaires and tech titans as Trump feted the leader of the Chinese Communist Party, even though he continues to assail Democrats for allegedly being communists. The president was eager to show Xi his under-construction ballroom that few voters support. Xi also seemed to feign interest when Trump gave him a tour of the Presidential Walk of Fame that he installed along the West Colonnade , complete with his predecessor Joe Biden depicted as an autopen. And then, as if the real spectacle wasn’t gaudy and elitist enough, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino posted an AI-generated video on social media that imagined him, his wife, and Trump family members at a champagne-soaked state-dinner after-party. Elon Musk promoted an even more ridiculous rendition. It all felt like a gift to Democrats, who pounced on the videos to paint those in the president’s orbit as dilettantes looking to enrich only themselves. Susan Del Percio, a longtime Republican strategist, told me that even Trump supporters who are concerned about the economy feel that the president no longer cares about them. “Voters are angry because they are hurting, and through his actions, Trump is telling them that he doesn’t give a damn,” she said. This week featured another event that likely will not land well with Americans who are struggling financially. Trump presided over a “Golden Age” event that featured business leaders and billionaires—and no talk of affordability challenges. Once more, Trump defended AI and even boasted that it would power a new government-services website. He then joked about where it stood among his accomplishments, saying, “If it is the biggest thing I’ve ever done, I’ve done a shitty job as president.” You can bet Democrats will grab that one too.

items.title: Baruch Obama
items.description: J osh Shapiro is having fun, and the crowd is loving it. “Let’s be clear,” the Pennsylvania governor says in his windup. Sometimes, instead of “let’s be clear,” it’s “let me tell you something.” He throws in some “y’alls” with a wide smile. The g ’s have fallen off his gerunds. He’s wearing a well-tailored dark suit, but no tie—his signature. When he gets going, his right index finger pokes the air. He’s almost bouncing as he pivots from one side of the audience to the other, in nearly perfect rhythm with his words. Then comes the crescendo; he’s shouting now, but only just loud enough to be heard above the roar of the crowd. Finally, the patriotic peroration—another signature. This one’s a story about Ben Franklin and that famous line: “A republic, if you can keep it.” He exhorts the audience to “show that this is not who we are as a nation.” That voice, that cadence—it’s all so familiar. Close your eyes, and you could almost imagine that you’re listening to the nation’s first Black president. But he’s the man who hopes to be the first Jew to win the White House. Shapiro, who is 53 and heavily favored to win reelection this fall, is one of several Democrats eying a 2028 White House campaign who have drawn—and even encouraged—comparisons to the 44th president. Like Barack Obama, Baruch Obama emphasizes pragmatism over doctrinaire progressivism; he has performed well in conservative areas of Pennsylvania that voted for Obama before turning to the right. Shapiro can wield a rhetorical knife, but he infuses his messaging with appeals to hope and optimism. [ Read: Josh Shapiro takes a gamble on his faith ] Yet the most obvious similarity is that when Shapiro gives a speech, he really sounds an awful lot like the Democrats’ most renowned speechmaker. It’s a once-you-hear-it-you-can’t-unhear-it type of thing, to the point where some Shapiro watchers believe he’s consciously imitating Obama. “He didn’t used to talk like this,” one Democrat who has closely followed Shapiro’s rise up the Pennsylvania political ranks told me, speaking on the condition of anonymity to avoid starting a public feud with the governor. Shapiro’s Obama echo attracted notice during the 2024 presidential campaign, when he was under consideration to be Kamala Harris’s running mate. “Is he doing an … Obama?” Ronny Chieng asked in a memorable roast on The Daily Show . J. D. Vance mocked him too. “He talks like Barack Obama,” Vance said on a podcast. “It’s like if I tried to do a really bad impression of Barack Obama.” Asked to respond to Vance at the time, Shapiro laughed off the charge. “Barack Obama was probably our most gifted orator of my time, so it’s kind of a weird insult,” he told reporters. My colleague Tim Alberta, in the profile he wrote of Shapiro earlier this year, documented the makeover that the governor underwent as he gained prominence—one that included a new hairstyle and sharper clothing as well as the Obama-esque way of speaking. “I just don’t hear it,” Shapiro told Alberta about the oft-noted comparison. “I don’t think I’ve changed my cadence or my rhythm or how I speak.” (A spokesperson for Shapiro declined to comment for this story.) Obama and Shapiro have known each other for two decades, and the younger Democrat has said that Obama set an example he has “tried to emulate.” Shapiro was an early endorser of Obama during his presidential run, and Obama joined Shapiro at a large get-out-the-vote rally in Philadelphia on the eve of his election as governor four years ago. (It was there that the Democrat I spoke with first noticed—along with many others—how closely Shapiro resembled Obama: “It was him and Obama back-to-back, and that was a moment where people were like, Jesus Christ .”) The two men have other things in common besides a speaking style. Both have owned dogs named Bo. And they both played basketball in their youth and remain huge fans of the sport. (Shortly after Lebron James signed with the 76ers, Shapiro said that he’d personally tried to recruit the NBA legend to Philadelphia.) Not everyone hears Obama when they listen to Shapiro. “I had never thought that,” Mike Mikus, a longtime Democratic consultant in Pennsylvania, told me. “He has a similar cadence, but I don’t think it’s a thing.” Mikus noted that politics “is a lot like football: Everybody steals from each other.” Shapiro, he suggested, also made a decent point in his rejoinder to Vance in 2024. “If you’re going to be compared to anybody, it sure as heck doesn’t hurt to be compared to the most popular figure in Democratic politics,” Mikus said. The Obama comparison certainly doesn’t appear to be hurting Shapiro in Pennsylvania, where a poll released last week by Siena University showed him leading his Republican opponent, Stacy Garrity, by 20 points. A boffo performance in November could propel him into the top tier of what is likely to be a crowded Democratic presidential field, especially if Shapiro’s coattails help his party flip Republican-held House seats and retake the majority. But he’ll face plenty of skeptics. Shapiro’s long-standing support for Israel is a liability with progressives who have demanded an end to U.S. aid for the Jewish state. Among swing-state overperformers, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona—former astronaut, husband to Gabby Giffords—has a more compelling biography, and Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia is a competitor for the Baruch Obama label:He’s also Jewish, he makes mainstream Democrats swoon, and, as my colleague Elaine Godfrey has noted , he can, when he gets revved-up, also sound a bit like Obama. [ Read: Who’s afraid of Josh Shapiro? ] Will Shapiro’s Obamaesque speeches inspire Democratic voters yearning for a charismatic communicator, or will they make him seem like a knockoff—an overeager pretender to the party throne? For an expert opinion, I consulted David Axelrod, the former Obama adviser, who has probably seen the ex-president deliver speeches as often as anyone alive. Like Mikus, Axelrod told me he hadn’t noticed the resemblance until people started pointing it out a couple of years ago. “He wouldn’t be the first person to try to emulate, or imitate, the president,” Axelrod said. He added that the ribbing Shapiro receives over his Obama-like stylings may end up being a funny footnote. But the association, should it burrow deeper in people’s minds, does carry risk for Shapiro. “Authenticity is the coin of the realm, and people want to know that you’re comfortable with yourself and that you’re being yourself,” Axelrod said. Voters crave it perhaps now more than ever.

items.title: 2027: Donald Duke better than all presidential candidates out there — Baba-Ahmed
items.description: The National Chairman of the People’s Redemption Party (PRP), Dr Hakeem Baba-Ahmed, says the party’s presidential candidate, Donald Duke, is the best contender in the field ahead of the 2027 general election, even as he admitted that candidate quality alone would not be enough to secure victory at the polls. Baba-Ahmed spoke in an interview with Arise News on Wednesday. “Candidate for candidate, we think we have the best. We’re very fortunate to have him. So, candidate for candidate, Donald Duke is better than all the candidates out there,” he said. He added, however, that the PRP was not banking solely on Duke’s credentials to carry the party to victory, noting that this realism was driving the party’s active role in ongoing coalition talks ahead of the election. “However, we’re realistic enough to know that just the quality of your candidate doesn’t just win the election, which is the reason why the PRP is in the frontline, right at the heart of this coalition building,” he said. Baba-Ahmed explained that the PRP’s push for a broader alliance of parties was being guided by consensus and constitutional processes, rather than an attempt to force Duke’s candidacy through on the strength of his profile alone. “We don’t want to prejudge or preempt anything by saying, ‘Because he’s the best, he has to be the candidate,’ by whatever means you come to do that. We want to build a coalition of parties that think the way we do,” he said. He stressed that the stakes of the 2027 election went beyond party interests, framing it as a decisive moment for the country’s trajectory. “Nigeria must, in the next four years, make a difference in the manner in which this country either develops or moves away from its fault lines, or just simply sinks into that. It really is that important,” Baba-Ahmed said. The PRP chairman’s comments come amid intensifying coalition-building efforts among opposition parties ahead of the 2027 presidential race, with Duke positioned as one of the figures around whom such an alliance could potentially coalesce. The post 2027: Donald Duke better than all presidential candidates out there — Baba-Ahmed appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GPL 2026/27: Kotoko face Karela test as Hamza Obeng takes temporary charge
items.description: Asante Kotoko will look to halt their recent slump when they welcome Karela United to Kumasi on October 1 in a Ghana Premier League fixture. The Porcupine Warriors have managed just one victory from their opening four matches and come into the game looking to recover from a damaging 2-0 home defeat by Aduana FC last Sunday. That result was frustrating for Kotoko, who played against 10 men for the entire second half and were unable to find a way back into the contest. Their early-season record now stands at one win, two draws and one defeat, leaving the Kumasi giants in need of a response. Thursday’s fixture will also mark the beginning of a new chapter for Kotoko following the departure of head coach Eric Tinkler. Young Porcupines coach Hamza Obeng is expected to oversee the first team on an interim basis as the club searches for a permanent successor. Obeng’s first assignment will be a potentially tricky encounter against a Karela United side arriving in Kumasi with confidence after beating Hearts of Oak 1-0 last weekend. Karela have shown attacking consistency this season, finding the net in each of their first four league matches. However, their form away from home has been a major concern. They have failed to win their last four league matches on the road, suffering three successive defeats after a draw. Karela have also conceded at least twice in each of those three defeats, while their most recent away league victory came against Dreams FC in February 2026. Kotoko, meanwhile, can draw encouragement from their record against Karela in Kumasi. The Porcupine Warriors have avoided defeat in their last six league meetings at home against Thursday’s opponents, recording three wins followed by three consecutive 1-1 draws. The game kicks off at 15:00 GMT at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium.

items.title: Le CRLDHT appelle à la libération immédiate de Abdallah Saïd
items.description: Le lundi 28 septembre 2026, la cour d’appel de Médenine a aggravé la peine prononcée en première instance contre Abdallah Saïd, la portant d’un à deux ans de prison ferme. Dans un communiqué publié le 30 septemnre 2026, le Centre pur le respect des libertés et des droits de l’homme en Tunisie (CRLDHT), Ong tunisienne basée à Paris, dénonce ce qu’il qualifie d’«une aggravation injuste et un acharnement contre la société civile». tout en exigeant sa libération immédiate, l’annulation de sa condamnation et l’abandon de toutes les poursuites. Arrêté le 12 novembre 2024, Abdallah Saïd a déjà passé près de deux ans en détention et devrait, sauf obstacle, être libéré dans les prochaines semaines. On espérait que l’audience du 28 septembre mettrait fin à une détention déjà longue de près de deux ans et annulerait la première condamnation. «L’aggravation de la peine au lieu de réparer l’injustice, est d’autant plus choquante que le ministère public avait lui-même fait appel du jugement de première instance. Elle confirme la détermination du pouvoir à frapper très fort la société civile», souligne le CRLDHT. Pour l’Ong, la procédure s’inscrivait dans « la campagne menée par les autorités contre les organisations de la société civile ». La peine d'Abdallah Saïd portée à deux ans de prison en appel «Initialement orienté vers le pôle judiciaire de lutte contre le terrorisme, le dossier en a été dessaisi faute de dimension terroriste. Les accusations d’atteinte à la sûreté extérieure de l’État et de blanchiment d’argent ont ensuite été classées à la clôture de l’enquête, au profit de chefs d’accusation à caractère financier. Ce glissement n’a pas empêché une condamnation encore plus lourde, ce qui renforce l’impression d’une justice instrumentalisée» , note encore l’Ong, qui rappelle «le caractère profondément humain et associatif du travail mené par Abdallah Saïd» , dont l’association qu’il dirige s’occupe des enfants atteints de la maladie dite «des enfants de la lune» . «Derrière cette condamnation, ce sont donc aussi des enfants atteints d’une maladie rare et particulièrement vulnérables, bénéficiaires d’un travail associatif essentiel, qui subissent directement les conséquences de cette répression» , souligne le CRLDHT, en rappelant la série de poursuites visant des actrices et acteurs de la solidarité et de la défense des droits, comme Cherifa Riahi, ancienne directrice de Terre d’asile Tunisie, libérée dans la nuit du 6 au 7 janvier 2026 après plus de vingt mois de détention ; Mustapha Jamali, directeur fondateur du Conseil tunisien pour les réfugiés, et Abderrazek Krimi, chef de projet, libérés après plus de dix-huit mois de détention, bien que leurs condamnations aient ensuite été confirmées en appel ; et Saadia Mosbah, toujours emprisonnée après la confirmation en appel de sa lourde peine de huit ans, dans un dossier fondé lui aussi sur des accusations financières et de gestion. I. B. L’article Le CRLDHT appelle à la libération immédiate de Abdallah Saïd est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Makkah Defence Alliance aims to 'bolster regional stability', says Saudi crown prince
items.description: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Wednesday said the Makkah Defence Alliance with Turkiye and Pakistan aims to bolster regional stability and shield the region from tensions and conflicts. He made the remarks while delivering the annual royal address on behalf of King Salman bin Abdulaziz during the opening of the third year of the ninth session of Saudi Arabia’s Shura Council. “To strengthen regional stability, shield it from the repercussions of tensions and conflicts, and coordinate efforts, the Makkah Defence Alliance was established between the kingdom, Turkiye and Pakistan,” the crown prince said. He added the alliance was part of efforts to strengthen security and stability in the region, expressing appreciation for the support of “brotherly and friendly countries” and their contributions to regional security and stability. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Makkah Mutual Defence Agreement on Aug 7 in Makkah. He said attacks targeting Gulf Cooperation Council countries demonstrate that Gulf security and stability are “indivisible.” He said Saudi Arabia is working with fellow Gulf Cooperation Council countries to safeguard them. The crown prince said Saudi Arabia has highly capable human and military resources able to confront and deter threats “regardless of their source.” He said the kingdom is making every possible effort to de-escalate tensions without compromising its security. “We will not hesitate to respond firmly to any threat or attack aimed at undermining our security,” he added. Mohammed bin Salman also said the establishment of a “multinational defensive maritime coalition” was aimed at strengthening maritime security and protecting common interests in international waterways. He rejected the use of international waterways as a tool for political or economic pressure. The crown prince also warned that “the world today is facing an energy crisis open to all possibilities.” He said Saudi Arabia has served as a “safety valve” for global energy security through its ability to provide oil supplies to international markets despite the escalation. He also condemned Israel’s “brutal attacks” against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and its “repeated violations” of Al-Aqsa Mosque . “We strongly condemn the continued brutal attacks by the occupying authorities against our brothers and sisters in Palestine, particularly in the Gaza Strip, as well as their repeated violations of Al-Aqsa Mosque,” he said. He urged the international community and the Peace Council to play their roles in reaching a lasting political solution in Palestine. “The kingdom’s commitment to the rights of the Palestinian people is a firm position and an ongoing effort that will continue until the Palestinian people obtain their legitimate rights, including the establishment of an independent state in accordance with international resolutions,” he said. On Yemen, the crown prince reaffirmed Saudi support, through the coalition backing the Yemeni government, for restoring government authority in the country and stability, while confronting Houthi attacks . He also reiterated Saudi Arabia’s support for Sudan’s unity and stability, the preservation of its state institutions and efforts to spare its people further suffering from war and destruction. Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis since March 2015, after the group took control of the national capital, Sanaa, and several provinces beginning in September 2014.

items.title: Flydubai : Israël évoque une tentative d'attentat, Trump raconte son échange avec Netanyahou
items.description: L'incident du vol Flydubai entre Dubaï et Tel Aviv prend une nouvelle dimension. Selon la version presentee par les autorites israeliennes, le copilote aurait poignarde le commandant de bord avant de tenter de precipiter l'appareil au sol. Le Boeing 737 a perdu plus de 4 000 metres d'altitude en quelques minutes avant d'etre stabilise puis deroute vers Tabuk, en Arabie saoudite. Flydubai confirme une « altercation » dans le cockpit, mais pas, a ce stade, le mobile avance par Israel. Benjamin Netanyahou affirme que des passagers et des membres d'equipage sont parvenus a penetrer dans le cockpit et a maîtriser le copilote. Le ministre israelien de la Defense, Israel Katz, parle d'une « tentative d'attentat terroriste djihadiste » destinee a provoquer le crash de l'avion. Le suspect serait de nationalite omanaise, selon un responsable israelien. Son identite, son mobile et une eventuelle appartenance a une organisation restent cependant a etablir. Trump reagit L'affaire est remontee jusqu'a Washington. Donald Trump a annonce avoir longuement echange avec Benjamin Netanyahou au sujet de l'incident. Selon le president americain, le copilote etait « peut-etre un terroriste » ou « peut-etre un cingle ». Trump a egalement relaye le recit selon lequel un passager israelien, presente comme plombier, aurait contribue a redresser l'appareil apres sa plongee. Il a toutefois lui-meme pris ses distances avec cette version : « Je ne sais pas si c'est vrai, mais c'est l'histoire que Bibi et quelques autres personnes m'ont racontee. » Netanyahou estime qu'une catastrophe comparable, par son ampleur potentielle, au 11 Septembre a ete evitee. Il affirme qu'Israel ne disposait d'aucun renseignement precis annoncant cette attaque et n'exclut, a ce stade, aucune piste concernant son origine. L'enquete menee notamment par les autorites saoudiennes devra desormais determiner si l'incident relevait d'un acte terroriste, d'une tentative de suicide ou d'un autre mobile.

items.title: We won’t return to ‘addictive’ fuel subsidy – Tinubu tells Nigerians
items.description: President Bola Tinubu has ruled out a return to Nigeria’s petrol subsidy regime, warning against calls to reverse his administration’s economic reforms. Tinubu spoke in his Independence Day address to Nigerians on Thursday, as the country marked its 66th anniversary, while defending the reforms introduced since he assumed office in 2023. The President acknowledged that the reforms had been difficult and that their “side effects were real”, but said abandoning them would amount to returning to policies that failed to address the country’s underlying economic problems. “Our reforms did not create the weaknesses in our economy. They confronted them,” Tinubu said. Tinubu said some “influential but regressive voices” were calling for a return to subsidy arrangements, describing such demands as an attempt to abandon the economic reforms. “Now, as certain influential but regressive voices would have us abandon the treatment and return ourselves to the abuse of addictive subsidies, we must resist their siren song,” he said. He said Nigerians should remember why the reforms were introduced and how far the country had come since then. Using a cancer-treatment analogy, Tinubu compared the Nigerian economy before the reforms to a patient whose condition had been allowed to worsen while successive governments focused on easing the symptoms rather than addressing the underlying problems. “Nigeria was like a sick patient who receives the terrible news that he has cancer,” he said. “His doctor explains that the treatment will be difficult and painful, but that it offers a strong prospect of recovery. The patient has a choice. He can begin treatment, endure its discomfort and fight the disease. Or he can ask only for morphine, dull the pain and leave the cancer to spread. “For too long, Nigeria’s leaders chose morphine while praying for a miracle that never came,” the president noted The post We won’t return to ‘addictive’ fuel subsidy – Tinubu tells Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigeria @66: Our greatest strength is the people — ADC chieftain, Nwosu
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu AWKA — Good governance advocate and former governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, in Anambra State, Mr John Nwosu, has said Nigeria’s greatest strength is its people, expressing optimism that the country can overcome its challenges and build a more prosperous future. Nwosu, in a message to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary, said the resilience, enterprise, creativity and determination of Nigerians had sustained the country through difficult periods. He, however, said citizens needed an environment that would allow those qualities to thrive. “I remain deeply convinced that Nigeria’s greatest strength is its people. Our resilience, enterprise, creativity and determination have carried this country through difficult times. “What Nigerians need is an environment that allows these qualities to flourish,” he said. Nwosu identified insecurity as the country’s most urgent challenge, urging those in authority to tackle criminality and ensure that citizens could travel, farm, trade and raise their families without fear. “Our most urgent challenge is security. Those in authority must tackle insecurity head-on. No citizen should be afraid to travel, farm, trade or raise a family because of criminality,” he said. He called for the deployment of modern technology, intelligence and better coordination among security agencies to prevent threats, protect communities and hold perpetrators accountable. Nwosu also advocated the use of technology to fight corruption and reduce waste in the public sector. According to him, digital procurement, transparent financial systems, electronic payments and real-time monitoring of public projects could make it more difficult to divert public resources. Beyond security and corruption, he urged leaders to address the everyday challenges facing Nigerians, including unemployment, rising living costs, inadequate infrastructure, unreliable power supply, healthcare deficiencies and limited opportunities for young people. He said young Nigerians deserved more than promises, stressing the need for quality education, practical skills, access to technology and an economy where hard work and enterprise could provide decent livelihoods. “I believe that public leadership must ultimately be about service, responsibility and results. We must build institutions that work, respect the rule of law and ensure that public resources are used for the common good,” he said. Nwosu said national renewal was not the sole responsibility of political leaders, stressing that citizens also had important roles to play. He urged Nigerians to reject corruption, protect public assets and contribute to the development of their communities. “As citizens, we must take our civic responsibilities seriously by electing credible, competent and accountable individuals. We must reject voter apathy and refuse to surrender our power to decide the future of our states and our country,” he said. On elections, Nwosu described voting as an opportunity for citizens to influence the direction of government and urged Nigerians to participate actively in the electoral process. “We must come out, vote, and where necessary, stand up to defend the integrity of our votes through lawful and peaceful means. “It is better to endure the inconvenience of an election day than to endure the consequences of a bad choice for four years,” he said. Nwosu urged Nigerians not to lose faith in the country, saying its challenges were real but that its capacity to overcome them remained strong. “On this Independence Day, my message is simple: let us not lose faith in Nigeria. Our challenges are real, but so is our capacity to overcome them. “I remain hopeful that, with courage, integrity, innovation and a genuine commitment to one another, we can build a Nigeria that gives every citizen a reason to believe in the future,” he said. The post Nigeria @66: Our greatest strength is the people — ADC chieftain, Nwosu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Morocco strike late to overcome 10-man Black Starlets
items.description: Morocco’s U17 side snatched a dramatic late victory over the Black Starlets, scoring with the last kick of the game to secure a 2-1 win in the second of two international friendly matches in Rabat. The Black Starlets, who played with 10 men for the greater part of the second half, were ultimately undone by a late counter-attack from the hosts. Morocco took the lead in the 11th minute after capitalising on a poor clearance from the Black Starlets goalkeeper. Ghana responded and created several opportunities to restore parity, with Issah Alidu coming close on three occasions after finding himself one-on-one with the Moroccan goalkeeper before the break. Ten minutes into the second half, the Starlets were reduced to 10 men when captain Abdul Rafiu Issah was shown a red card for a strong tackle on a Moroccan attacker. Despite the numerical disadvantage, the Black Starlets continued to push forward in search of an equaliser. Their persistence paid off in the 75th minute when Yaw Acheampong produced a free-kick to bring Ghana level. Gavi Robinho came close to completing the comeback when his effort was blocked by a Moroccan defender and diverted for a corner. However, Morocco quickly turned defence into attack from the resulting corner, launching a counter-attack that ended with the hosts scoring with the final kick of the match. The result leaves the two-match series honours even, with Ghana having won the first encounter 2-0 before Morocco claimed the second game. The matches conclude the Black Starlets’ international preparations ahead of the WAFU Zone B U17 Championship, which also serves as the qualifying tournament for the 2027 U17 Africa Cup of Nations.

items.title: Israel president to present ‘heroism’ awards to 4 flydubai passengers
items.description: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Thursday he would present “heroism” awards to four Israelis who helped overpower a flydubai co-pilot and prevented him from crashing the plane they were on. “You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster. Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society,” Herzog, who holds a largely ceremonial role, said in a statement. “I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.” He also hailed the plane’s Indian pilot, Smit Machchha, who Israeli officials say managed to open the cockpit door to let passengers and crew save the plane after being stabbed by the co-pilot. Among the Israelis to receive the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism is Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber who says he beat and pinned down the co-pilot after breaking into the cockpit. Yanoun, wearing a still-bloody shirt, was personally welcomed on his return to Israel Wednesday at Ben Gurion Airport by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The passengers said they rushed to the cockpit after a woman screamed and said there was a stabbing. “It was an extraordinary incident,” Asaf Rajuan, who helped pin down the attacker and will also receive the award, told Herzog, according to the president’s office. “We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct: to survive, to save the family, the people, and the children.” AFP The post Israel president to present ‘heroism’ awards to 4 flydubai passengers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Syrie : sept morts dans l’attaque d’un bus à Homs
items.description: Au moins sept personnes ont ete tuees et quatre autres blessees le mercredi 30 septembre dans l'attaque d'un minibus civil dans la province de Homs, dans le centre de la Syrie . Des hommes armes ont ouvert le feu sur le vehicule alors qu'il circulait sur le pont de Masyaf, selon l'agence officielle Sana et les autorites sanitaires locales. Le bus transportait des employes qui rentraient de leur travail. Selon une source securitaire citee par l'AFP, il s'agissait notamment d'ingenieurs et d'ouvriers d'une entreprise privee du secteur de l'electricite. Les blesses ont ete hospitalises. Aucun groupe n'a revendique l'attaque et les autorites n'ont, pour l'heure, identifie ni les assaillants ni leur mobile. Une enquete a ete ouverte. Des terroristes toujours actifs en Syrie L'attaque intervient dans un contexte securitaire toujours fragile, pres de deux ans apres la chute de Bachar el-Assad . Le nouveau pouvoir d'Ahmed al-Chareh tente de retablir l'autorite de l'etat dans un pays marque par quatorze annees de guerre, la circulation des armes et la persistance de groupes clandestins. Les autorites doivent notamment lutter contre les cellules de Daesh, tout en faisant face a d'autres foyers de violence. Plusieurs incidents recents illustrent cette instabilite. En août, une explosion visant un bus des forces de securite pres de Damas avait fait plusieurs blesses, tandis qu'un attentat contre un bus a Jaramana avait blesse 14 personnes. En juillet, deux explosions avaient egalement frappe les abords d'un hotel de Damas. Les autorites avaient ensuite annonce l'arrestation d'une cellule accusee d'en etre responsable. L'attaque de Homs survient enfin alors que des infrastructures energetiques ont recemment ete visees. Un gazoduc a notamment ete touche pres d'une importante centrale electrique dans la region de Damas . a ce stade, aucun lien n'a toutefois ete etabli entre ces differents incidents.

items.title: Nyaho-Tamakloe calls on Kurt Okraku to resign amid Black Stars struggles
items.description: Former Ghana Football Association Chairman Dr Nyaho Nyaho-Tamakloe has called on current president Kurt Okraku to resign amid the Black Stars’ ongoing struggles. The senior national team suffered a 4-2 home defeat by The Gambia in their second Group C qualifier, surrendering a two-goal advantage at the Accra Sports Stadium. The defeat came after the Black Stars had already lost their opening qualifier against Ivory Coast, leaving them without a point from their first two matches. Ghana are now bottom of Group C, with Ivory Coast and The Gambia leading the group on six points each. The results have increased concerns about Ghana’s chances of reaching the 2027 AFCON, with the country now facing the possibility of missing the tournament for a second successive time under the current administration. “If he feels that he has failed and he has the culture of resignation, then nobody will tell him he will resign by himself as I did when I was there,” Nyaho-Tamakloe told Citi FM. “If he is not coming up with good results, that’s why I use the word culture of resignation, there are certain things you don’t force on people. “Either you do it and then one will know exactly that this man is principled…he should just quit like others have done in the past,” Dr Nyaho-Tamakloe added. Ghana will face Somalia in their next AFCON qualifier in November, with the Black Stars needing a positive result to improve their position in Group C. The Black Stars have won just one of their last eight matches in all competitions.

items.title: Un mercredi législatif : chronique d’une observatrice
items.description: Mercredi 23 septembre 2026, il est 7 heures lorsque je referme derrière moi la porte de la maison. Dehors, le soleil est déjà levé, et la ville s'étire, à demi endormie encore. Je prends la route pour Skhirat. Dans le silence du matin, la voix de Medi 1 s'élève de la radio et égrène les chiffres du jour: le nombre d'inscrits, le nombre d'observateurs accrédités, les bureaux prêts à ouvrir leurs portes. Tout un pays mis en nombres, comme un avant-goût du grand jour. Je dois être à 7h30 devant un collège, celui où l'on m'a affectée comme observatrice du Collectif Associatif pour l'Observation des Élections (CAOE). Ce jour-là, l'école n'attend pas d'élèves. Elle attend des électeurs. J'arrive à l'heure dite. Deux gendarmes me laissent passer sans un mot. J'entre. Pour l'occasion, le collège abrite trois bureaux de vote, trois salles de classe où se tient, pour un jour, une sorte de moussem civique. Le portail, lui, prend son temps. Il ne s'ouvre qu'à 7h53, pour laisser les premiers électeurs patienter à l'intérieur, et le vote ne commencera qu'à 8 heures précises. À 8 heures sonnantes, ils sont quatre. Quatre silhouettes déjà là, fidèles au rendez-vous, comme on l'est aux choses qui comptent. Au même instant, le Cheikh de Skhirat traverse la cour et lance, du ton dont on annoncerait un match: “Bdat l'3amaliya, al ikhwan”, “L'opération a commencé, les frères”. Dans mon bureau, nous sommes huit à veiller sur une urne. Il y a le président du bureau, épaulé d'une assesseure et d'une secrétaire de bureau. Il y a aussi une représentante du Parti de la justice et du développement (PJD), un représentant du Rassemblement national des indépendants (RNI) et un observateur du Conseil national des droits de l'Homme (CNDH). Et, près de la sortie, un monsieur, feutre non effaçable à la main, trace sur le doigt de chaque votant cette petite marque d’encre violette typiquement marocaine, qui atteste qu'on a voté. Deux partis rivaux, deux regards indépendants, une équipe pour faire tourner la machine: un petit Parlement réuni autour d'une boîte transparente. Toutefois un Parlement assez singulier, où les partis se reconnaissent moins à leurs idées qu'à leurs dessins. Les représentants eux-mêmes, comme la plupart des votants, ne connaissent des partis qui se présentent que leurs emblèmes. Leurs noms, eux, ne disent rien à personne, ni en arabe, ni en français. Le Parti de la justice et du développement (PJD) ? Personne ne l'appelle ainsi: c'est la lampe, al misbah. L'Union socialiste des forces populaires (USFP) ? Le nom entier ne suscite qu'un regard vide, puis, à la vue du logo : “Ah, la rose violette !”, Lwarda. Le Rassemblement national des indépendants (RNI) ? La colombe, Lhmama, tout simplement. Le Parti authenticité et modernité (PAM) ? Le tracteur, bien sûr. Des symboles, plus que des programmes. Vers 8h30, la salle se vide. Personne ne se présente, la journée commence à peine. Le bureau s'accorde alors une parenthèse de dix à quinze minutes, le temps d'un petit-déjeuner: thé à la menthe sucré, olives noires et baguettes de pain. Les portes du bureau demeurent ouvertes. Le rituel, lui, se répète d'un votant à l'autre. On présente sa carte nationale, et elle seule: l'original, jamais une photocopie, ni un passeport, ni aucun autre document. On cherche le nom dans la liste. Mais ce nom, que la loi veut entendre prononcé à voix haute et distincte, est à peine murmuré, quand il est dit. Puis vient le bulletin, que l'électeur ne prend pas lui-même: on le lui tend. Puis, très vite, une phrase s'installe dans la salle, et ne la quittera plus : “ Dir(i) krwa west l'carreau li aajbek”. “Fais une croix dans la case qui te plaît”. Je l'ai entendue tant de fois que j'ai fini par la tenir pour un indicateur à part entière. Beaucoup ne savaient pas comment remplir le bulletin, quoi cocher, ni comment. Et la distinction entre le vote local et le vote régional semblait échapper à la plupart. D'autres ignoraient jusqu'à leur bureau de vote. Ils allaient de l'une à l'autre des trois salles, leur carte d'identité à la main, comme on cherche son chemin dans une ville étrangère. Et puis il y a eu cette femme. Elle est venue voter sans même être inscrite. Rien, dans son attitude, ne trahissait la conviction. On aurait dit qu'elle rendait service à quelqu'un, qu'elle s'acquittait d'une commission, comme on dépose un colis. Voter pour voter, au hasard. Elle n'était, au fond, que la figure la plus nette d'une impression qui ne m'a plus quittée: beaucoup semblaient venus rendre un service, bien plus qu'accomplir un devoir. À mesure que les heures passent, le portrait se dessine de plus en plus. Il vient presque autant de femmes que d'hommes. Mais la salle a les tempes grises: la plupart ont franchi la quarantaine. Les 18-24 ans, eux, se comptent sur les doigts des deux mains, une dizaine tout au plus, sur une journée entière. Rien de surprenant car à l'échelle du pays, cette génération ne pèse plus que 4 % du corps électoral. Mais il y a loin entre lire un chiffre dans un rapport et le voir, en chair et en os, dans un bureau de vote. À 12h45, c'est à mon tour de quitter la salle. Mon propre bureau de vote se trouve à une vingtaine de minutes de là, et je ne pouvais me résoudre à passer cette journée à regarder les autres voter sans accomplir moi-même, pour la toute première fois, ce devoir. Je m'éclipse donc, brièvement. Le bureau ne reste pas sans regard, l'observateur du CNDH et les représentants des partis demeurent à leur poste. Je vote, et je rentre aussitôt. À 13h30, j'ai regagné ma place à Skhirat, le pouce marqué, à mon tour, de ce petit sceau violet. À 14h45, un grand camion franchit le portail et s'avance jusque dans la cour de l'école. On en descend un vaste plat de poulet rôti à la marocaine, des sodas et du pain. Un festin démocratique. Or rien, ce jour-là, ne devait interrompre le vote. De 8 heures à 19 heures, le scrutin est censé se dérouler d'un seul tenant, sans pause: chaque électeur doit pouvoir entrer, à toute heure, et voter. Le repas se tient donc au milieu du scrutin, et son parfum se répand bientôt jusqu'aux électeurs, qui confient, en entrant glisser leur bulletin, avoir senti l'odeur du poulet. Les partis, eux, ont aussi leur intendance. Au fil de la journée, des paniers arrivent pour leurs représentants: le panier du PJD d'un côté, celui du RNI de l'autre. Chacun nourrit les siens. De tout ce qui se passe, ces représentants ont été, comme moi, les témoins. Ils sont restés là, du matin au soir, à regarder. Mais eux, contrairement à moi, n'étaient pas tenus au silence. Là où mon rôle se bornait à remplir, en silence, mon formulaire d'observation, eux avaient le droit de parler, de signaler, d'interpeller le président du bureau. Ils n'en ont pourtant rien fait. Pas une remarque, pas une réserve. Vers 17h30, la salle se remplit d'un coup. Une demi-heure durant, jusqu'aux alentours de 18h30, les électeurs se succèdent sans répit, c'est le pic de la journée. Après les heures creuses de l'après-midi, on dirait que la ville s'est souvenue, au dernier moment, du rendez-vous. La file s'allonge, et avec elle revient la même question, “Kifach ndir ?”, (“Comment je fais ?”), suivie de la même réponse, inlassable: “Dir(i) krwa west l'carreau li aajbek”. “Fais une croix dans la case qui te plaît”. À 19 heures précises, les portes se ferment et les urnes s'ouvrent. Le dépouillement ne s'achèvera qu'aux alentours de 23h30. Sur 464 inscrits, 188 sont venus, soit quatre sur dix. Vient alors l'heure de vérité, et avec elle une évidence amère: tous les votes ne compteront pas. 40 bulletins sont annulés pour le scrutin local, 46 pour le régional. Certains portent des signes ou des mots griffonnés, d'autres des croix qui débordent de leur case. Près d'un votant sur quatre s'est déplacé, a patienté, a présenté sa carte, est reparti le doigt marqué de violet, pour une voix qui ne pèsera pas. La phrase entendue tout au long du jour prend alors tout son sens: elle n'a pas suffi… Ces scènes ne relèvent pas de l'anecdote. Je les ai vues se répéter, heure après heure, et elles disent quelque chose de plus grand que ce bureau. Dans cette salle de Skhirat, c'est précisément là que tout vacillait: un bulletin que l'on ne savait pas lire, deux votes que l'on ne savait pas distinguer et des partis que l'on ne reconnaissait qu'à leurs dessins. Le bulletin, à mes yeux, doit devenir lisible pour tous, et la différence entre vote local et vote régional doit être expliquée, simplement, avant même d'entrer dans l'isoloir. Car entre la loi électorale et l'électeur, il manque un maillon, le plus simple peut-être : l'explication. Et derrière l'explication, un manque plus profond encore: la conscience. La conscience de ce que l'on fait en glissant un bulletin dans l'urne, et de pourquoi on le fait. Car ce jour-là, j'ai eu le sentiment que beaucoup étaient venus comme on vient pour rendre un service, et non comme on accomplit un devoir citoyen. Cette conscience ne naît pas un matin d'élection. Elle se cultive, patiemment, par l'éducation civique, la pédagogie démocratique et tout au long des cinq années d'un mandat, pas seulement dans l'agitation fébrile des derniers jours de campagne. On ne peut pas espérer d'un citoyen qu'il comprenne en une semaine ce qu'on a négligé de lui expliquer pendant cinq ans. Il y a d'ailleurs une ironie à le constater dans un collège: c'est entre ces murs mêmes que cette leçon devrait s'enseigner, bien avant que l'on y vienne voter. Ce mercredi-là, j'ai compris qu'un scrutin peut se dérouler dans les règles, et laisser pourtant des citoyens repartir sans savoir tout à fait ce qu'ils ont fait de leur voix, ni pour qui, au fond, ils l'ont donnée. La participation se mesure en pourcentages. La compréhension, elle, attend encore qu'on la mesure. The post Un mercredi législatif : chronique d’une observatrice appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Plus de 600 interpellations dans les lycées : élus débordés, risque de dérapage
items.description: La mobilisation des lyceens pour des remplacements de professeurs et davantage de moyens gagne du terrain. Avec plus de six cents arrestations en une seule journee et des elus sous pression, la contestation, deja emaillee de violences , pourrait basculer. Un mouvement qui s'etend et se radicalise Le mouvement a touche 356 etablissements le 30 septembre, soit pres d'une vingtaine de plus que la veille, selon le ministere de l'Interieur. Pour la seule journee, 625 personnes ont ete interpellees et 83 policiers ou gendarmes blesses. Depuis le debut des blocus, 119 eleves et personnels ont ete blesses, a indique le ministre de l'education edouard Geffray. Édouard Geffray, sur le blocus des lycées : «119 élèves et personnels ont été blessés depuis vendredi dernier» Toute l'info est à retrouver sur https://t.co/NVs1Rf6rXd pic.twitter.com/9JlSdsUmCC — CNEWS (@CNEWS) September 30, 2026 L'IGPN a ete saisie de trois enquetes apres des blessures de lyceens a Sevran, Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone et Tours, ou un jeune a ete hospitalise pour des lesions « compatibles » avec un tir de lanceur de balles de defense (LBD). Le ministre de l'Interieur Laurent Nuñez a pourtant juge les interventions « proportionnees » et a renouvele ses instructions aux prefets et a l'ensemble des services de securite interieure. J’ai renouvelé mes instructions aux préfets et à l’ensemble des services de sécurité intérieure suite à l’intensification des troubles à l’ordre public et à un climat de violence inacceptable aux abords des établissements scolaires. Je leur renouvelle toute ma confiance pour… pic.twitter.com/w3fWOOqzpa — Laurent Nuñez (@NunezLaurent) September 30, 2026 Lors d'une conference de presse commune le 30 septembre a Paris avec l'Union etudiante, le president de l'Union syndicale lyceenne, Ryad Rani, a appele a un « acte deux » de la mobilisation. Il a reclame un « financement massif des lycees et des universites » et invite « toutes les organisations syndicales, associatives et politiques » a les rejoindre jeudi et le 6 octobre. L'Unef a de son cote appele les etudiants « a descendre dans les rues partout en France ». Après plusieurs jours de mobilisation, la jeunesse est sortie massivement dans la rue hier. Il faut que la mobilisation s’intensifie, rendez-vous le 6 octobre dans la rue ! pic.twitter.com/HlGo1zSwe0 — UNEF (@UNEF) September 30, 2026 Ce mot d'ordre a trouve un echo : les adherents de l'Union etudiante et de l'Unef sont ainsi convies a manifester ce 1ᵉʳ octobre et le 6 octobre, contre la suppression de places en fac et le gel des APL. Les elus, eux, peinent a contenir la tension. a Saint-Denis, le maire LFI Bally Bagayoko a cree la polemique en affirmant que « la violence, a un moment donne, peut etre legitime », avant d'appeler a la desescalade, alors que le parti melenchoniste est en pointe dans la contestation . Le prefet a signale ses propos. Sur X, Jean-Luc Melenchon a repondu : « Les Insoumis appellent a la non-violence des methodes de lutte. […] Le gouvernement doit repondre aux revendications ». Les lycéens mobilisés, lorsqu'ils ont la parole, sont clairs sur leurs revendications : plus de moyens pour leur éducation. Ils sont souvent soutenus par leurs équipes éducatives, en première ligne face au délabrement de l'école publique. Les insoumis appellent à la non-violence… — Jean-Luc Mélenchon (@JLMelenchon) September 30, 2026 Emmanuel Macron, depuis Madrid, a lui martele qu'« aucune de ces craintes ne legitime la violence » et que les responsables politiques ne sont « pas la pour agiter les peurs ». Des feux de poubelles, tirs de mortiers et barricades ont emaille plusieurs villes. Le gouvernement a annonce une « plateforme de concertation » pour recueillir les revendications lyceennes, avec une restitution nationale promise par edouard Geffray. Mais face a l'extension du mouvement et aux appels a l'« acte deux », la question demeure : jusqu'ou ira la colere ?

items.title: 2027: I’ll resign if Nigeria doesn’t change in one year — Amaechi
items.description: Vice-presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, Rotimi Amaechi, has vowed to resign from office if Nigeria fails to begin witnessing significant changes within one year of the party assuming power in 2027. Amaechi made the declaration in an interview on AIT’s Democracy Today on Wednesday, saying an ADC administration would prioritise security, education and the economy. He said tackling corruption would also be central to addressing the country’s challenges, arguing that public funds meant to address critical sectors were being diverted into private pockets. “We must deal with three things. We must deal with security; we must deal with education; we must deal with the economy. And to do all that, corruption will have to come down because there’s no money for anybody to steal,” Amaechi said. The ADC candidate also criticised the removal of fuel subsidy by the administration of President Bola Tinubu, arguing that Nigerians had not benefited sufficiently from the policy. “President Tinubu remove subsidy, what are the benefits of subsidy? Subsidy money is in private pockets and they are celebrating,” he said. Amaechi also expressed concern over the contrast between widespread poverty and the lavish parties he said he encounters in parts of the country. He said he sometimes spent only a few minutes at such events because he questioned the source of the money being spent, given the level of poverty in Nigeria. “I sit down and ask myself, where are these people getting this money from, going by how high poverty is in Nigeria?” he said. On the economy, Amaechi said Nigeria is heavily dependent on imported finished goods, claiming that the country now imports more than 46 per cent of such goods. “Who are those importing? Nigeria is in trouble,” he said. The ADC vice-presidential candidate also referred to reports of Nigerians booing President Tinubu during his arrival at the Lagos International Airport, saying an ADC government would change the situation. “I watched people hoot at Tinubu from the Lagos International Airport to his house. If we become President, nobody will do that, they will be clapping for us because we will change Nigeria,” he said. Amaechi’s one-year pledge comes shortly after his political rival, Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, said President Tinubu should remove him from office if he fails to deliver the FCT to the President in the 2027 election. Amaechi, however, said he was prepared to stake his own position on the performance of an ADC government. “This time, I will say it. If Nigeria does not begin to change one year after we’ve come to office, come to me, I will resign,” he said. The post 2027: I’ll resign if Nigeria doesn’t change in one year — Amaechi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Societe Generale Group agrees to sell Ghana subsidiary to Attijariwafa Bank
items.description: Société Générale Group has signed an agreement with pan-African banking group Attijariwafa Bank to sell its majority stake in Société Générale Ghana. Under the agreement, Société Générale Group will divest its entire 60.22% stake in the Ghanaian subsidiary. Attijariwafa Bank will acquire a 55.22% stake, while the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT) will acquire the remaining 5%. The transaction will result in Attijariwafa Bank taking over all activities currently operated by Société Générale Ghana. It will also take over the bank’s client portfolios and employees within the entity. The proposed divestment remains subject to the fulfilment of customary conditions precedent and approval by the relevant financial and regulatory authorities. The agreement marks a major change in the ownership structure of Société Générale Ghana, with Attijariwafa Bank set to become the new majority shareholder once the transaction receives the required regulatory approvals.

items.title: Court nullifies Ali Isa JC’s APC ticket, orders fresh Balanga/Billiri primary
items.description: …bars ex-Chief Whip from fresh contest, orders withdrawal of Certificate of Return By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe GOMBE — The Federal High Court No. 2 sitting in Gombe has nullified the emergence of Hon. Ali Isa J.C. as the All Progressives Congress, APC, candidate for the Balanga/Billiri Federal Constituency in the 2027 House of Representatives election. The court, presided over by Justice Vera E. Ibrahim, also ordered the APC to conduct a fresh primary election for the constituency within 30 days and barred Isa from participating in the exercise. It further ordered the withdrawal of the Certificate of Return issued to Isa by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, following the disputed primary. The judgment followed a suit filed by Hon. Alfred John Atajiri, who challenged Isa’s eligibility to participate in the APC primary and the validity of the process through which he emerged as the party’s candidate. A major issue in the suit was the timing of Isa’s membership of the APC and the party’s compliance with statutory requirements governing the conduct of primary elections. According to the judgment, as reported in the account of the proceedings, Isa joined the APC 16 days before the primary, while his name was not contained in the party’s membership register submitted to INEC within the period prescribed by law. The court relied on Section 77 of the Electoral Act 2026, which requires political parties to submit their membership registers to INEC at least 21 days before conducting their primaries. Justice Ibrahim consequently held that Isa’s participation in the primary was invalid, unlawful, null and void. The court also found that the primary did not comply with relevant statutory requirements, including claims before it that the exercise was not conducted in some parts of the constituency. Consequently, the court nullified the primary that produced Isa and directed the APC to conduct a fresh exercise in compliance with the Electoral Act and other applicable requirements. Salary, benefits controversy Another issue raised during the proceedings concerned Isa’s continued status in the National Assembly and the receipt of salaries and other benefits. The issue formed part of the broader legal challenge concerning his eligibility and participation in the APC nomination process. However, the principal orders of the court focused on the validity of his participation in the APC primary, the withdrawal of his Certificate of Return and the conduct of a fresh primary. Political implications The judgment has altered the APC’s nomination process for the Balanga/Billiri Federal Constituency, with the party now required to organise another primary among eligible aspirants. Although Atajiri instituted the suit that resulted in the judgment, the court did not award the APC ticket to him. Instead, it ordered the APC to conduct a fresh primary through which the party’s candidate for the constituency will emerge. Isa had emerged as the APC candidate after the party’s May 16, 2026 primary. Reports from the exercise indicated that he defeated other aspirants, including Atajiri and Saratu Hamman Jauro. The latest judgment has, however, nullified that primary, subject to any further legal action arising from the decision. APC faces 30-day deadline The APC is now required to conduct a fresh primary within 30 days in compliance with the court’s order. The party will also be expected to comply with statutory requirements on membership registers, the eligibility of aspirants and the conduct of the primary. The judgment underscores the importance of compliance with electoral laws and party rules as political parties prepare for the 2027 general elections. The court’s decision does not determine who will emerge from the fresh primary. Rather, it nullifies the earlier process and directs the APC to conduct another exercise in accordance with the law. The affected parties may also pursue available appellate remedies. Pending any further order from a higher court, the operative directives of the Federal High Court are that Isa’s emergence from the earlier primary is nullified, his Certificate of Return is to be withdrawn, he is barred from the fresh primary and the APC must conduct another primary within 30 days. The post Court nullifies Ali Isa JC’s APC ticket, orders fresh Balanga/Billiri primary appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 1 killed as under construction Red Line structure collapses on Karachi’s University Road
items.description: KARACHI: A security guard was killed on Wednesday after an under-construction bridge structure of the Red Line project collapsed near Baitul Mukarram mosque in Gulshan-i-Iqbal, according to a Rescue 1122 spokesperson. The deceased was performing security duties at the site when the structure collapsed, the spokesperson said. A Rescue 1122 team was dispatched to the site after the Central Command and Control Centre received the report, the spokesperson added. The collapse comes as work on the Red Line project continues. Last week, Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon said efforts were underway to complete the ongoing work and restore traffic flow on University Road. The stalled construction on the Red Line had resumed in November 2025, after the removal of several bottlenecks following the chief minister’s intervention. Meanwhile, thousands of University Road commuters continue to face daily hardships. Designed to cover around 27 kilometres from Malir Halt to Numaish via University Road , the BRT Red Line project was announced in 2017 with an initial cost of around Rs79 billion. After commencement of the work in early 2022, the project was initially scheduled for completion by 2023, which was later pushed to 2024 and subsequently extended to the end of 2026. Various factors have been cited by officials to justify these delays, including disputes with contractors, safety stoppages, rising construction costs due to depreciation of the rupee, difficulties in land acquisition, relocation of utilities and coordination failures between implementing agencies.

items.title: Five things to know about the Nobel Prize
items.description: Since 1901, the Nobel Prizes have been awarded to individuals and organisations for work leading to great advances for humanity, in line with the wishes of the prizes’ founder, inventor Alfred Nobel. The 2026 winners will be announced between October 5 and 12, starting with the Nobel Prize in Medicine on Monday from 11:30 am (0930 GMT). Here are five things to know about the prizes and their founder. – In detention – Since 1901, five Nobel Peace Prize laureates have been prevented from attending the awards ceremony in Oslo. In 1936, German journalist and pacifist Carl von Ossietzky was detained in a Nazi concentration camp. Myanmar opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi was under house arrest when she won the prize in 1991. Given permission by the junta to travel, she declined for fear of potentially not being able to return to her country. In 2010, Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo was in prison. His chair remained empty, where the prize was placed. In 2022, Belarusian human rights campaigner Ales Bialiatski was in jail. He was represented by his wife Natalia Pinchuk. In 2023, Iranian activist Narges Mohammadi was held in Iran’s Evin prison when the prize was awarded. – Young and old – In 2014, 17-year-old Pakistani human rights activist Malala Yousafzai became the youngest winner of a Nobel Prize. Another unusually young laureate was Australia’s Lawrence Bragg, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with his father in 1915 when he was 25, for work carried out at the age of 21. Iraqi Nadia Murad was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 25 in 2018 for her efforts on behalf of the Yazidi minority. In contrast, American John Goodenough was the oldest to become a Nobel laureate. He won the Prize in Chemistry in 2019 at the age of 97 for his work on the lithium-ion batteries that power smartphones and electric cars. The year before, his compatriot Arthur Ashkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics at the age of 96. – Posthumous awards – Since 1974, the statutes of the Nobel Foundation stipulate that the prize may not be given posthumously. But the prize may still be awarded if the recipient dies between the time of the announcement in October and the formal prize ceremony in December. Before the change, only two people had won a Nobel posthumously. One was Dag Hammarskjold, the Swedish secretary-general of the United Nations, who died in a plane crash in 1961 but was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize later the same year. And in 1931, the Nobel Literature Prize was awarded posthumously to another Swede, poet Erik Axel Karlfeldt. In 2011, the committee for the Nobel Prize in Medicine selected Ralph Steinman of Canada, unaware that he had passed away just three days before the announcement. The foundation nevertheless gave him the award. – Women laureates – Only 68 of the 633 Nobel prizes awarded since 1901 have been given to women, representing about 10 percent, though the share has been steadily increasing since the early 2020s. The science fields have the lowest representation of women laureates. The various committees that award the prizes have repeatedly refused to introduce quotas, instead encouraging nominations of women scientists. Only five women have won a Nobel physics prize out of a total of 230 laureates in the discipline, three out of 99 economics laureates, eight out of 200 chemistry laureates, and 14 out of 232 medicine laureates. Marie Curie was the first woman laureate in 1903 and she is to this day the only woman to have received two Nobel prizes, first for physics in 1903 and then in 1911 in chemistry. – Nobel the poet – Nobel went down in history as the inventor of dynamite but he also loved English poetry and was an admirer of Percy Bysshe Shelley and Byron. He wrote poetry himself his entire life, sometimes in his native Swedish but mostly in English. In a letter to a friend, he wrote: “I have not the slightest pretension to call my verses poetry; I write now and then for no other purpose than to relieve depression, or to improve my English.” In 1862, at the age of 29 and questioning his literary talent, he sent a letter in French to a young woman that said: “Physics is my field, not writing.” In 1896, the year of his death, he wrote a scandalous tragedy in four acts titled “Nemesis”, inspired by Shelley’s play “The Cenci” about a woman in 16th-century Rome who murders her incestuous father. The post Five things to know about the Nobel Prize appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Réforme du système de santé au Maroc : plaidoyer pour passer de la couverture administrative à l'accès réel aux soins
items.description: Cinq ans après le lancement de la refonte globale du système de santé national et de la généralisation de l'Assurance Maladie Obligatoire (AMO), sous l'impulsion de la vision royale, le bilan est riche en avancées structurelles, mais marqué par un défi majeur : transformer les progrès législatifs et financiers en un réel vécu quotidien pour le citoyen. C'est le constat dressé par le Dr Tayeb Hamdi, médecin et chercheur en politiques et systèmes de santé. Dans une étude d'évaluation analytique, le spécialiste souligne que l'effort financier consenti par l'État est incontestable. Il rappelle en ce sens que le budget de la santé a fait un bond spectaculaire, passant de 19,7 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) en 2021 à 42,4 MMDH prévus pour 2026, soit un doublement en cinq ans. Parallèlement, l'immatriculation à l'AMO a connu une avancée administrative majeure, couvrant 32 millions de personnes en 2025, soit 88 % de la population marocaine. Pourtant, le Dr Hamdi met en garde contre l'illusion des chiffres, en ce sens que « la généralisation de l'AMO est une réussite administrative majeure, mais l'assurance ne doit pas rester une carte dans un portefeuille, elle doit devenir une vraie clé qui ouvre le parcours de soins » . De fait, le chercheur révèle qu'en réalité, seuls 25,6 millions de citoyens bénéficient d'un accès effectif. Près de 8,54 millions de personnes — soit près d'un citoyen sur quatre — demeurent exclues de l'accès réel, bloquées par le phénomène des « droits fermés » qui touche notamment 65,72 % des Travailleurs Non-Salariés (TNS) et 43,11 % des souscripteurs à l'AMO Chamil. Le deuxième écueil mis en évidence par l'étude concerne le mur financier du « reste à charge ». Selon les données du Dr Hamdi, les ménages financent encore plus de 52 % des dépenses totales de santé, dont 38 % en paiement direct au moment de la maladie. Ce reste à charge en ambulatoire atteint 50,2 % à la CNSS et 41,1 % à la CNOPS, principalement en raison de Tarifs Nationaux de Référence (TNR) obsolètes, inchangés depuis 2006. Conséquence directe de cette déconnexion : 41,5 % des Marocains renoncent encore aux soins pour des raisons économiques. L'étude pointe également la crise de confiance qui fragilise l'hôpital public, que le spécialiste qualifie de « colonne vertébrale du système ». Les chiffres de l'AMO traduisent cette fracture : 91 % des remboursements captés vont au secteur privé, contre seulement 9 % au secteur public. L'analyste souligne par ailleurs la pénurie structurelle en ressources humaines avec un déficit de 30 000 médecins et de plus de 60 000 soignants, aggravé par un exode médical où plus de deux médecins quittent le Maroc chaque jour, et une concentration de 75 % des professionnels dans seulement trois régions. Face à ces menaces sur la soutenabilité financière du système, illustrées par des remboursements dépassant les cotisations de 121 % à la CNOPS et de 172 % pour les TNS,, le Dr Tayeb Hamdi appelle à un « Engagement National ». L'expert résume ainsi l'enjeu central de cette étape décisive : « le citoyen doit devenir à la fois le point de départ et le point d'arrivée de la réforme ». Il préconise notamment la révision urgente des TNR, la généralisation du tiers payant en ambulatoire, l'instauration d'un forfait national de prévention pris en charge à 100 %, et la réduction du reste à charge des ménages sous la barre des 30 % d'ici 2028, puis 25 % à l'horizon 2030.
